# Progress Thresholds and Progress Item Decision Record

The initial issue appeared after a batch of progress items arrived and the terminal position did not advance one cell at a time based on the item count. The follow-up started at `src/click/termui.py`. Near the issue, `progress`, `pending`, `count` and `pos` were visible, but received updates, buffered updates, and screen changes were not recorded separately at the time.

Two approaches were compared:

- Advance and render directly whenever each completed item arrives. The behavior is intuitive, but it may produce many small changes.
- Keep small updates in the progress object first, then advance after reaching a minimum step. This reduces refreshes, but we need to confirm who stores the count and when it is cleared.

The decision this time is to continue investigating the second approach first, without treating caller-side aggregation as the decided implementation. If each caller determines its own threshold, different entry points may retain different remaining counts; if an entry point does not return the final small batch, the completion record and position may diverge.

The early working hypothesis remains "advance immediately for every completed item." It is only being used to plan the first check and cannot later be treated as a behavioral conclusion. When the first frame shows no change, it is not yet possible to determine whether no update was received, the position did not change, or rendering happened later.

The direct dependencies visible in the file header are `inspect`, `io`, `itertools`, and `os`. These references lead the reader near the module, but are not enough to show which caller produced the progress item.

Open: Does `update_min_steps` affect the screen or the internal position? What happens when the final segment does not reach the threshold? We need subsequent observations from the same input, not just the first frame or final screen.

# Progress Thresholds and Progress Item Decision Record

## Separate the two first

The draft treated "receipt of a completed item" and "movement of the progress bar" as the same action. During the review for 2024, the observation method was changed first: one observation only checks whether the progress item enters the progress path, while the other checks whether `pos` changes. After that, the absence of a new position in the terminal could no longer be directly interpreted as the update not having been received.

The review used the same set of inputs for two observations. The first only left evidence that the update had entered the relevant path; only the second provided a chance to compare the state before and after accumulation. The first frame can show that the first processing took place, but cannot by itself show whether the threshold was triggered. The old draft's claim that "every completed item advances immediately" remains an early hypothesis and is no longer a troubleshooting conclusion.

## Three placement options

There were three options on the table at the time.

The first was to change `pos` directly on every update and then pass it to rendering. It is the easiest way to infer a visual change from a single item, but it cannot explain the interval in which the count has already advanced while the position temporarily stays put.

The second was for `ProgressBar` to retain small batches of updates and merge them into an advance once the count reached `update_min_steps`. This keeps the display cadence near the progress object, so callers do not each need to implement their own threshold check. This approach can explain "received but not yet moved," but there were not enough snippets at the time to confirm how the remainder is handled at the end.

The third was for the caller to aggregate first and then pass a larger quantity to the progress object in one operation. It may reduce internal state, but it distributes threshold and tail handling across multiple entry points. There was no evidence at the time that all legacy callers would return the remaining quantity.

This round's decision is to continue investigating the second option. The reason is not that it already covers all entry points, but that it can accommodate the difference between the two observations and avoids scattering the same display strategy across callers. The caller-first aggregation option remains unadopted.

## Constraints left by the review

A single `completed` log cannot substitute for observing the position. Completion events are on the input side, position changes belong to the progress object, and terminal redraw is recorded at another layer. Looking only at the final position can show that an accumulation at some point took effect, but cannot show whether a buffering stage existed in between.

The note at the time was:

> Do not use the first frame to judge threshold behavior. The first frame only shows what happened in the first observation.

The minimum call log should retain at least one below-threshold update and the subsequent update that triggered actual movement. If only the final screen is stored, it is impossible to tell whether the quantity was not accumulated or whether the position had already changed but rendering arrived late.

## Rejected older claims

An earlier draft suggested moving the threshold check into the caller because the caller knows how many items it received in one operation. The review did not adopt this. Once multiple entry points each retain their own uncommitted count, threshold behavior depends on each entry point's own completion timing; this weakens the progress object's role as a unified observation point.

Another claim was that "if `completed` appears in the logs, the display can be considered complete." This has been crossed out. It collapses the input event and the visible result into a single judgment, which is exactly what caused the first investigation to misread the situation.

## Tail handling still undecided

This version still has not confirmed how to handle the final small batch. If the accumulated amount remains below `update_min_steps`, we need to see whether the exit path passes through the same advancement logic; the existing review did not preserve enough local snippets. It has also not confirmed the actual caller corresponding to `progress item observation`; the entry point, version, or ownership cannot be inferred from the location of `src/click/termui.py`.

The next round should record the order of the input items, the counts before and after the threshold check, changes in `pos`, and the state of the buffered quantity after advancement. Only then can this decision be cross-checked separately against the actual entry's result.

# Decision Record on Progress Thresholds and Progress Items

This page was not written as a specification in one pass. It began with a record of "completed items not advancing one by one," and was later overlaid by several reviews, one rerouting, and a neighboring to-do item. The old judgments remain below because they explain why input, position, and terminal output were treated as the same thing at the time.

The fixed starting point for looking back is `src/click/termui.py`. The repository index lists it as an existing Python module, and the file header shows:

```text
import inspect
import io
import itertools
import os
```

These direct dependencies and the file location can guide readers toward progress-related objects. They do not provide a list of upstream callers, nor can the path alone identify which entry point a progress item comes from. An early record phrased "the issue name points to this file" as though it meant "the caller is right here." That inference was later withdrawn; the path remains as a starting point for looking back, but the attribution does not.

## The First Sentence on the Old Page

The earliest recorded working hypothesis was: each time a completed item is received, the progress position should increase; if the terminal does not change, first suspect that rendering did not run. This hypothesis was useful for planning a quick check, but it collapsed three points in time into one: the update arriving, the progress object changing its internal position, and the terminal displaying a new screen.

Item-by-item advancement and small-batch advancement were compared at the time. Item-by-item advancement is easy to explain: seeing an item leads to expecting a visible action. Small-batch advancement might draw fewer frames, but it raised a question that had no answer at the time: who stores the uncommitted count, how is it incorporated into the position once the threshold is reached, and will the remainder still be handled on exit?

The first draft chose to investigate small batches rather than immediately require callers to change. Having callers aggregate first also appeared capable of reducing refreshes, but it handed control of the display cadence to each entry point. There was not enough evidence at the time to prove that all entry points would handle the remaining count in the same way, so this was listed as a candidate, not a decision.

The conclusion retained verbatim from the early section is:

> Every completed item advances progress immediately; investigate under this assumption for now.

**Later overturned.** This sentence represents only the initial working hypothesis. It cannot serve as a description of the current implementation, nor can an unchanged first frame be used to infer that "the update did not happen."

## The Split After Review

The next review did not ask for the whole page to be rewritten as a unified explanation. Instead, it asked for the observations to be separated. The first section records only whether updates enter the progress path; only the second section records whether the position changes. Both sections use the same set of inputs, to avoid mistaking differences caused by different inputs for threshold effects.

During the review, three places to handle updates were reconsidered: changing `pos` directly on every update; having `ProgressBar` temporarily buffer short updates itself; and having callers combine items before handing them over. Changing `pos` directly is the most straightforward option, but it cannot explain the interval in which "the counting action has already appeared, while the display or position has not changed yet." Caller-side aggregation can make caller-side logs shorter, but requires every caller to understand the threshold and responsibility for the remainder. Buffering inside the progress object adds one more state, but keeps the display cadence close to the same object.

The local decision at that point was to continue checking the second approach. Here, the scope of "decision" was very narrow: decide to look inside the progress object for the cumulative relationship at the next step, not announce that all entry points had been verified. The old approach remained on the page so it would be clear why it was not adopted.

The review note was very brief:

> Check the second observation first; the first frame cannot settle the matter.

The first frame may only be the output of initialization or the first processing step. It cannot replace an observation taken after accumulation, nor can it show that the temporarily stored quantity has been cleared. Storing only the final display is also insufficient, because the final position may have changed without leaving any intermediate state.

## Two observations from the year 2024

The review in 2024 year split the same group of progress items into two records. The first observation saw count-related actions but did not see the position advance item by item according to the item count; actual advancement appeared only in the second observation, after accumulation. This result invalidated the debugging premise that "every completed item advances immediately," but it did not cover the exit path.

At the time, the names of the stored fields and their values before and after cleanup were not printed one by one. Therefore, the record could only go this far: quantities below the threshold appear to remain in the object, and a position change is seen only after the threshold is reached; whether the final small batch is processed in a follow-up step still requires tracing the termination path. The appearance of movement in the second observation is not enough to mark all remaining processing as known behavior.

This round also eliminated an overly broad logging conclusion: the appearance of `completed` does not mean display completion. A completion log shows that an event occurred on the input side; a change in `pos` shows that the progress object performed a position update; whether the terminal has been redrawn still depends on the output side. The three results are adjacent, but they are not different ways of writing the same field.

The previous proposal for caller-side aggregation was explicitly marked as not adopted at this point. The issue was not only that invoking Fang Ke allowed each caller to determine a different threshold, but also that there was no unified place to hold the remaining quantity. If one entry point returns the remainder before ending while another ends directly, caller-only logs will produce two different interpretations.

## Meeting side notes that did not become an interface

The subsequent discussion added no new interface and left only one disagreement. One view regarded the threshold as a purely terminal-output policy; the other held that if the position itself is also delayed, it must be possible to find the uncommitted quantity in the progress object. Both sides agreed that the next record could not capture only the first frame.

The meeting note required `pending`, `count`, and `pos` to be placed in the same minimal call-log excerpt. This was a logging method, not a new field convention. It was used to distinguish whether the quantity had entered the object, whether the accumulation had reached the threshold, and when the position changed. No complete implementation diagram was left behind, nor was any caller marked as confirmed.

After this discussion, "progress-item observation" was divided into two closely related questions. One was how the progress object handled the quantity it received; the other was which actual entry point was still using this observation method. The former could be traced further near the module, while the latter could not be inferred from the file location or issue name.

## Retained old debugging diagram

The following diagram was once used to explain why people initially expected every item to show a visible change:

```text
item completed -> pos + 1 -> render
```

**Deprecated.** It presents completion events, position advancement, and rendering as consecutive and inevitable actions, which does not match the gap between the two observations. But the diagram was not deleted because it accurately represents the initial misreading.

Another candidate diagram is:

```text
caller counts items -> ProgressBar receives total -> render once
```

**Not adopted.** It could serve as a design for reducing refreshes, but it would make the caller responsible for thresholds and tail handling. It is not evidence of the progress object's current behavior.

There is also a shorter old record:

```text
first observation: no visible move
last observation: position moved
```

This only shows that the before and after displays differ; it does not show whether what happened in between was accumulation, advancement, or delayed rendering. This is why later records require the two observations of the same input and the relevant counts to be presented together.

## Two entry points reopened in 2025

`CLK-201` was reassigned in the historical action on 2025-09-08, with the reason given as "The main changes now are to Progress rendering; switch to someone on this side to continue." This rerouting brought attention back to the rendering path, but did not change caller ownership from unknown to known.

The next day, the card became blocked. The recorded reason was that it was waiting for a second progress observation with the same input, to avoid conflating the first frame with threshold-based advancement. The public comment only confirmed that progress threshold accounting in the Progress rendering section was still unconfirmed, and requested that the input and output be kept in the minimal call log. It supports continued observation, not filling in the missing exit result for this page.

`CLK-218` retains the adjacent `progress item observation` issue. The card asks for a caller that still uses this observation method to be found, and then for the actual version, entry point, and current result to be checked. It makes the target of the investigation clear, but does not mean that the caller has already been found.

These two card entry points cannot be combined into a conclusion that "all sources have been verified." The former points to threshold rechecking and the rendering path; the latter points to actual adopters. The page can link to them separately, but each one's unresolved scope must still be retained.

## The current decision concerns the object's internals

In a later focused check, the accumulation relationship inside the progress object was narrowed down to the following current formulation:

ProgressBar batches updates below update_min_steps by retaining the pending count in _completed_intervals, then advances pos by the accumulated amount and clears _completed_intervals when the threshold is reached.

This rule only determines the order among short updates within the progress object, accumulated advancement, and cleanup. It does not determine how the upstream code produces a progress item, identify the caller for `CLK-218`, or answer how each exit path handles the remainder below the threshold. It appears after the legacy approach and review traces because those historical layers explain why this statement cannot be derived directly from the first frame.

Breaking this decision down, updates below `update_min_steps` do not immediately become visible progress counted by item; the pending amount remains in `_completed_intervals`. Once the accumulated amount reaches the threshold, `pos` advances by the accumulated amount, and the temporarily stored value is cleared after the advancement completes. This describes the internal state relationship of the progress object, not the complete timing of terminal output.

The corresponding local state diagram is as follows:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending: update below update_min_steps
    Pending --> Pending: retain pending count
    Pending --> Advanced: accumulated update reaches threshold
    Advanced: pos advances by accumulated amount
    Advanced --> Cleared: clear _completed_intervals
```

`Pending`, `Advanced`, and `Cleared` are reading labels in the diagram, not new fields. The diagram only represents updates below the threshold, advancement after the threshold is reached, and cleanup. When the first frame becomes visible, when the terminal redraws, and whether residual amounts are processed on exit still cannot be inferred from this diagram.

## What this decision does not cover

First, the final batch that does not reach the threshold. The current materials contain no separate exit-path fragment, so they cannot show how all exit methods handle it. "Cleared after the threshold is reached" cannot be extrapolated into "always topped up on exit."

Second, the actual caller. `src/click/termui.py` is a fixed starting point for follow-up searches, not a caller registry. The file-header dependencies only show which libraries the module directly references; they cannot show which entry point is still using progress item observation.

Third, the first frame and terminal output. The internal accumulation relationship is already clearly defined, but whether the first frame displayed the state before accumulation and whether the output occurred after the position changed still need to be checked against local logs for the same input. The final display cannot replace this process.

IV. Ownership of other modules.DOC-11 records a separate API review topic; this page retains it only as an adjacent document when related materials need navigation, and does not carry the completion callback contract judgment into the progress object decision.

## Current verification steps

When entering from `src/click/termui.py`, first locate the progress object's update action, then record separately which actions `pending`, `count`, and `pos` each appear in. Do not collapse the three into a single line saying "progress update." The minimum sample should include one below-threshold update and one observation after the threshold is reached for the same input, with the first frame and subsequent output kept separate.

If the log contains only the first frame, mark it as insufficient observation; if it contains only the final position, mark it as missing the cumulative process. If the record shows that a staged count exists but does not show cleanup after advancement, retain only these two local facts. Do not fill in the missing segment with the expected exit behavior.

For `progress item observation`, the verification must leave this module, find the actual usage point, and then check the entry point, actual version, and current result. `CLK-218` remains a navigation and investigation direction, not completed proof from the caller. For the threshold issue, `CLK-201` can bring back a historical review, but its blocking record also shows that the second observation cannot be omitted.

## Notes still attached beside the old paragraphs

**Deprecated: force every item to refresh, then use the screen to infer the default behavior.** This temporary approach can make the change more obvious, but it changes the cadence being observed. At most, it shows that a rendering branch can display something; it cannot prove that the default path advances item by item.

**Deprecated: compare only the final `pos`.** The final position may show that the cumulative count eventually took effect, but it does not show why nothing moved the first time or whether anything was staged in between. It cannot independently support an explanation of the first frame.

**Not adopted: caller-side aggregation.** This option is still worth retaining among the historical options because it can indeed reduce the number of deliveries; however, it delegates the threshold and tail to the caller, which does not conform to the local decision within the object already made on this page.

**Adjacent issue: progress item observation.** Completing the responsibility table is not part of this page's incidental scope. The card requires the actual entry point, version, and result; those on-site materials are not currently available, so this stops at the object pending investigation and the navigation point.

## Excerpt from the old meeting

> Set the first frame aside for now. We need to see whether the second run with the same input advances.

> Do not split `pending`, `count`, and `pos` across three log segments.

> When you see completed, record the input first; do not directly write that the display completed.

These sentences are traces of the observation plan at the time, not new interface text. They explain why two rounds of observation were retained later, and why this page does not treat the final view as the sole evidence.

## Appendix: Examples Still Not Removed

### Single-item progression example

```text
item completed -> pos + 1 -> render
```

Deprecated. It works as a sample of early intuition, but not as a diagram of the current implementation.

### Caller aggregation example

```text
caller counts items -> ProgressBar receives total -> render once
```

Not adopted. It was a candidate for reducing refreshes and internal state, but the fact that the caller bears responsibility for the tail count kept it from becoming this page's decision.

### Two-end observation example

```text
first observation: no visible move
last observation: position moved
```

The evidence is too brief. It remains in the appendix because this is exactly the judgment that early logs can easily produce: the before and after differ, but there is no intermediate accumulation or cleanup action.

### File entry example

```text
src/click/termui.py
  progress / pending / count / pos
```

This small index only indicates where to start reading. It does not turn the module path into caller ownership, nor interpret the four imports at the top of the file as a complete execution chain.

Two questions still remain unresolved by this decision: whether the remaining amount below `update_min_steps` at exit follows the same processing path; and which real entry point is still using progress item observation. They require, respectively, the end-path fragment and the adopter's version, entry point, and result; they cannot be answered on their behalf using the current object's internal terminology.

# Completion Callback and First Progress Frame Proposal

This proposal still concerns only a partial interface of `src/click/core.py`. It does not attempt to infer the full call chain from the file location; what can currently be confirmed is the file header's direct dependencies and adjacent terms such as completion, context, callback, and argument. Parameter sources, help text, and edge cases around default values have already been placed in DOC-12; keeping them here would merge two reviews into one entry point.

The initial draft only asked "What does the callback receive?" and put progress first-frame visibility in the same section as an aside. This creates a practical problem: readers may interpret whether the first progress frame is visible as behavior the completion callback is required to handle. The second version therefore split the two threads apart, but still did not fully spell out the costs of the candidate options. This version preserves that evolution, and narrows the current recommendation accordingly.

The public callback contract will use the following wording:

> An Argument can use a shell_complete callback that receives the invocation context, parameter, and incomplete token and returns completion candidates for the current command line.

This wording puts responsibility on the inputs and outputs between Argument and the callback. The invocation context, parameter, and incomplete token are the inputs the callback needs to determine the candidates; the candidates are returned as completion results for the current command line. It does not additionally specify display width, ordering, error text, or the first progress frame; those should not be implicitly treated as the same protocol through a single callback contract.

There are still two options. A is to keep a thin entry point: the entry point passes through existing objects, the callback returns candidates, and the caller continues to handle the result within its own boundary. The benefit is a narrow interface meaning, with context, parameter, and token available for direct comparison during review; the cost is that different callbacks may handle candidate display details differently. B is to add a normalization wrapper at the command layer: after receiving the callback result, the entry point converts it into a unified structure. The benefit is centralized formatting; the cost is that the wrapper layer takes on new compatibility responsibilities, and the migration scope also expands if existing callers already depend on implicit conversion.

The current proposal selects A for trial, but only at the interface boundary; it does not also decide the candidates' specific line format or error-handling policy. If later investigation finds that existing callers must depend on a unified display structure, propose a separate migration plan for B; do not modify this narrow contract just to fill out the format. If it cannot be confirmed that a parameter already exists at the entry point, leave it as an unresolved item rather than filling the gap with a speculative adapter layer.

`progress first-frame visibility` remains separate. It needs to answer when the first progress result is observed and whether that observation is affected by the completion path. The existing material is insufficient to commit on this page to a threshold, refresh timing, or terminal behavior, so the proposal retains only this boundary: the completion callback's inputs and outputs cannot automatically substitute for a progress display protocol. If the two later turn out to share execution adjacency, they should be re-reviewed using a new code excerpt or result, rather than backfilling speculation into the old paragraph.

Withdrawal conditions should also be handled by boundary: if review finds that A would force the entry point to let the callback decide the display structure, withdraw only the "thin entry point" trial option, not the problem definition that the callback receives the context, parameter, and incomplete token; if it finds that the first progress frame needs a separate lifecycle-control scheme, withdraw only the assumption that both can be covered by the same proposal. During rollback, retain the existing invocation entry point and do not add an unconfirmed wrapper layer.

There are three unresolved items: whether the candidates' public representation already has a stable shape; whether errors should be exposed inside the callback or at the entry point; and whether existing callers depend on implicit conversion. They affect format compatibility, error boundaries, and migration cost, respectively. Until these checks are complete, this page can serve as a basis for interface review, but it cannot replace a review of the specific call relationships.

# Troubleshooting tree: parameter sources and literal defaults in help

The earliest notes recorded two observations that shouldn't be conflated: a literal default appearing in help, and getting a `value` after an invocation finished. The first is displayed text; the second is the result of parameter processing. Identical text doesn't mean they came from the same input path.

The investigation started at `src/click/core.py`. Near the top of the file, you can see `errno`, `inspect`, `os`, and `sys`. These are just landmarks for finding the same file next time, not evidence of a parameter's source.

Start by capturing evidence as follows:

```text
Default text appears in help
├─ Full help output is available
│  └─ Check default / default_map in the parameter declaration
└─ Only a secondhand account is available
   └─ Record the reported display behavior first

A value is observed after execution
├─ A prompt occurred
│  └─ Record what happened before and after the prompt, and the final result
├─ Command-line input was provided
│  └─ Record the original argument positions and the final result
└─ The input sequence is incomplete
   └─ Don't determine the source
```

The early habit was to find the parameter declaration first, then look at the final `value` and guess whether it looked like a default or user input. That order was barely workable when the values differed; once the default, prompt input, and command-line input happened to produce the same literal value, there was no way to infer the input path from the result.

When help output and runtime results both appear, open two records first. Keep the full original help output, not just one line; for a runtime issue, keep the input sequence, not just the final value. If either layer is missing, stating what hasn't been seen yet is more useful than filling in a conclusion about the source.

There was also a margin note about a state directory that had not been pre-created. No result from the same invocation was available at the time; the note only asked that, the next time a similar case came up, someone record whether the directory had already been pre-created. It is neither the cause of a change in help text nor evidence of a parameter's source.

# Parameter Source and Literal Defaults: Troubleshooting Tree

The previous version recorded the help page's literal default separately from the post-run `value`, but during actual reviews people still used a shortcut: extract the default text from the help page, compare it with the final value, and record the source as default if they match. The problem with this method isn't the string comparison; it skips the input process.

This time, troubleshoot through two windows. The display window answers only what the user saw on the help page and which default-related settings appear near the corresponding declaration. The runtime window answers only whether a prompt occurred, whether there was explicit command-line input, and what the final `value` was. The two windows can coexist, or either can stop on its own; don't force them together just to make the record look tidy.

## Display Window

Save the complete help output first. Extracting only the line containing default often loses the surrounding explanation, leaving later readers unable to tell whether it was ordinary text, a default description, or a position change after formatting. Then locate the corresponding parameter declaration from `src/click/core.py`, and record separately whether `default` and `default_map` are present.

When `default` is present, you can confirm that the declaration contains a default-related setting; when the help page shows the same literal value, you can only confirm that the two pieces of evidence can be compared side by side. Do not use this to write "this run used the default." Help output is display-layer evidence and cannot replace the input record for an invocation.

When `default_map` is present, retain the mapping content and the text shown to the user on the help page separately as well. Both relate to the default, but that does not mean they are the same object. If neither appears in the declaration, stop the display window here: retain the original help text and parameter location, wait for a real invocation, and do not infer the source from the text.

The file entry point is still `src/click/core.py`. Keep `errno`, `inspect`, `os`, and `sys` as adjacent items visible during navigation; do not use them to draw a parameter-processing call graph. Older records treated "found the file" as if it meant "found the call." Do not use it that way this time.

## Runtime Window

When the runtime value is abnormal, first ask whether a prompt occurred. If an interactive prompt occurred, put the state before the prompt, the input after the prompt, and the final `value` in the same record. When only the last line of output is available, the prompt input is easily misrecorded as the default value.

Next, look for explicit command-line input. Record the original argument position here, not just the parsed result. Defaults, prompts, and command-line input can all produce the same string; once the original position and interaction history are lost, the final value cannot distinguish them.

Only then revisit the parameter declaration. `default` or `default_map` in the declaration can be recorded as candidate sources, but they do not prove that this source was used by the invocation. If the input entry point cannot be recovered, record only "default-related declaration visible; source for this run unconfirmed."

The state directory that was not preconfigured should still be recorded separately under the environment conditions. It may appear in the same report, but the existing records do not contain a complete invocation linking it to the help output or to a source change. Do not elevate the directory state into an attribution.

## Deprecated Shortcut

The following old section is retained for reviewing old records:

> Extract the default text from the help page; if the final `value` is the same, record the source as the default value.

This wording no longer applies. It records neither the prompt nor the command-line input position, so it cannot rule out different entry points producing the same value. If an old ticket was closed this way, first check whether the original help text, parameter declaration, prompt record, or raw command-line input is still available. If there is no supplementary evidence, do not polish the old conclusion into a definitive judgment.

## Field Tree

```text
Abnormal report
├─ Help page text only
│  ├─ Found default
│  │  └─ Save the declaration and complete help output
│  ├─ Found default_map
│  │  └─ Save the mapping and display text; record them separately
│  └─ Found neither
│     └─ Stop at the display layer
├─ Runtime result only
│  ├─ Prompt record available
│  │  └─ Save the before-and-after prompt states and final value
│  ├─ Explicit command-line input available
│  │  └─ Save the input position and final value
│  └─ Input entry point unknown
│     └─ Record candidate sources only
└─ Both help and runtime are abnormal
   └─ Save the two sets of evidence separately; do not combine the attribution yet
```

A stopping point in the tree does not mean the issue must be closed. It indicates which layer no longer has enough evidence for further judgment. When the display window lacks a real invocation, continue to retain the display observation; when the runtime window lacks the input process, continue to retain the result. When supplementary evidence becomes available, add it to the corresponding window; do not reconnect the two sides by matching equal strings again.

If the report says only "the default value looks wrong," first restore any one of the help output, raw command-line input, or prompt record. Without original evidence, the record may still be useful, but it cannot select a source on behalf of the invocation.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Parameter Sources and Literal-Default Help

This page grew out of a very short note on parameter handling. Paragraphs left from the early days, reminders later written in the margins while on call, one unsuccessful attempt at backward inference, and several reviews of gaps in the cards are all still in their original places. They are not conclusions reached at the same time. When older text conflicts with requirements further down, first confirm the circumstances that text belongs to, then continue along the current branch.

The path used to locate the entry point has always been `src/click/core.py`. The early records only copied `errno`, `inspect`, `os`, and `sys`, which were visible near the top of the file; these imports were not later expanded into relationships in parameter handling either. They only help the investigator return to the same file. The help output, the input process for an individual run, and the final result still need to be filled in with evidence from the actual case.

## 2023-12-25: The Initial Separate Records

What initially caused confusion was not a clear implementation failure, but two similar reports: some people said the help page showed a literal default, while others said the `value` at the end of a run did not seem to come from the expected source. Early records tried to group both under "default value issues," but it soon became clear that the same literal value could appear in completely different places.

The working rule retained at the time was to first distinguish what was being observed. For help-page issues, record only the text the user saw and the settings near the parameter declaration; only for runtime issues should the input method and final result be recorded. This rule did not explain the full semantics of the source object or provide a final conclusion for every branch, but it already prevented the most direct confusion: help text is not evidence of an individual run.

The tree from the old note is shown below. It can still be read as a starting point, but it is not today's complete procedure:

```text
Seeing literal default help
├─ Save the original help-page text
├─ Find default / default_map near the parameter declaration
└─ No actual invocation
   └─ Record only what is displayed

Seeing the value after a run
├─ There is prompt interaction
│  └─ Save what happened before and after the prompt
├─ There is command-line input
│  └─ Save the input location
└─ Neither is clear
   └─ Do not guess the source
```

This record deliberately did not include "the help text and the final value are the same" as a branch. Such a match shows, at most, that the reader saw the same string in two places; it cannot show where the string entered parameter handling for this run. Early cases often lacked the complete invocation, and forcing a connection between the two places would only make subsequent evidence conform to an attribution that had not been observed.

## Margin Note for 2024-03: Directory State Is Only a Condition

An old page-margin note once said: when you encounter a state directory that has not been pre-provisioned, also record whether the directory has already been pre-provisioned. That note did not include an actual invocation, user-visible output, or the parameter input process, so it was never a conclusion that "the directory caused a help anomaly."

Later, someone treated two records—the directory condition and the simultaneous appearance of literal default help—as causal. After review, all we can confirm is that they co-occurred; we cannot confirm that the former changed the latter. That judgment has been crossed out, while the original reminder remains: directory state can help distinguish cases, but it cannot replace help output or override prompt or command-line input.

If the report contains only a screenshot, the directory state can be written next to the screenshot conditions; if the report includes a complete invocation, it can only be listed alongside the prompt and explicit parameter values. Without a result from the same invocation, do not elevate this condition to a cause.

## 2024-11-11: Separate the display layer from the runtime layer

The later review did not immediately resolve the source issue; it first changed how the records were kept. The display layer focuses on what is actually shown on the help page, as well as the visible `default` and `default_map` in the parameter declaration. The runtime layer focuses on whether a prompt occurred during the invocation, whether explicit command-line input appeared, and what the final `value` was.

After separating them this way, the two sets of evidence no longer need to be equally complete. A help-page anomaly may have only the complete help output and the declaration; a runtime-value anomaly may have only the input process and the result. If either set of evidence is incomplete, that does not prevent the other from being retained. What must actually be avoided is filling a missing item in one window with a string from the other window.

### The old display-layer procedure

First, save the complete original help text, rather than extracting only the line containing default. The surrounding explanation may determine whether that text is an ordinary description, a default-related display, or a formatted result. Then return to `src/click/core.py` to find the corresponding parameter declaration, and record separately whether `default` and `default_map` are visible.

When `default` appears in the declaration, all we can currently confirm is that the parameter has an adjacent default setting. The help page happening to display the same literal value does not mean that this run used it. When `default_map` appears in the declaration, the mapping content and the help text must also be retained separately; do not transcribe one as the other merely because both are default-related information.

If neither appears in the declaration, stop the display-layer analysis here. Stopping here only means that no further display-layer evidence is available for determining the source. The help output must still be retained, and the parameter location must still be recorded; it is simply not possible to infer from the help text an invocation that either never occurred or was not recorded.

### The old runtime-layer procedure

When runtime results are anomalous, first check whether a prompt occurred. If one did, the state before the prompt, the value obtained after the user input, and the final `value` should be placed in the same record. Keeping only the last line can easily make prompted input look like a result provided by default.

Next, look for explicit command-line input. The original argument position should be saved together with the final value. The default, prompted input, and command-line input may happen to leave exactly the same string; without the position and process, the entry point cannot later be recovered from the string alone.

Only then review declarations related to defaults. A declaration can be listed as a candidate source, but it cannot testify for a particular invocation. If there is no prompt record and no command-line position in the available evidence, the more accurate conclusion is "candidate setting visible; source for this invocation unconfirmed."

The branch diagram from that time can still be used to collect evidence:

```text
Anomaly appears
├─ Help page shows literal default text
│  ├─ Has default
│  │  └─ Save the declaration and the original help text, then review the runtime evidence
│  ├─ Has default_map
│  │  └─ Save the mapping and displayed text; do not merge the fields
│  └─ No default-related setting found
│     └─ Stop at the display layer and wait for the corresponding invocation
├─ Runtime value is suspicious
│  ├─ Has prompt
│  │  └─ Save the state before and after the prompt and the final value
│  ├─ Has explicit command-line input
│  │  └─ Save the original position and the final value
│  └─ Input entry point missing
│     └─ Record only the candidate, not the source for this invocation
└─ Both types of phenomenon appear
   └─ Keep two separate records; do not merge the attribution prematurely
```

## 2024-12: Failed quick reverse inference

This section describes the old approach and is retained because some early records still use it.

> Extract the default text from the help page and compare it with the final `value`. If the two strings are identical, record the source as the default value.

At the time, this path seemed convenient: a report often included both a help screenshot and the final result, so transcribing them was enough to write an answer. Later review found that the records did not capture whether a prompt occurred, nor the position of any explicit command-line input. The string comparison itself did not fail; what failed was treating the missing input process as proof that it did not exist.

Therefore, this old approach has been deprecated. It cannot serve as the current stopping condition, nor can it be rewritten as "fast mode" and continued. For an old report closed out using this approach, first check whether the original help text, parameter declarations, prompt process, or command-line input is still available. Without additional evidence, the old conclusion can only be retained in its temporal context; it cannot be presented as an already confirmed fact.

This reverse inference also left an operational lesson: when the help page and runtime result are anomalous at the same time, they should not be given the vague name "default value error." Save both sets of evidence first, then determine whether they are related. Once an issue name presupposes a source, subsequent records will naturally ignore inputs that do not match that name.

## 2025-09-23 to 2025-09-24: Tracing parameter sources

CLK-203 was later linked to a support case. The public record immediately afterward still noted that one point regarding parameter source provenance remained unconfirmed; it was then passed to the current module maintainer because they had already reviewed the existing implementation. What this provides is an entry point for tracing and an unresolved status; it cannot be read as evidence that a specific invocation had been reproduced.

When starting from this card, first confirm whether the report concerns the display layer or the runtime layer. If the material brought back is from a help page, save the complete output and compare it against the parameter declarations; if it is a runtime report, look for the prompt, explicit command-line input, and final `value`. If all you have is a secondhand account, stop at this branch rather than treating the support link itself as a substitute for invocation details.

The review note written during that review remains here:

> "Mark the unconfirmed points first; finding the implementation entry point does not mean the input process has been reconstructed."

This is not a new definition of a source, but a correction to an old habit. File paths can help locate the object, and parameter declarations can provide candidate settings; what actually distinguishes one invocation from another is still the prompt, explicit input, and corresponding result at the time.

## 2025-10-17 to 2025-10-20: The gap in literal default help

The record for CLK-220 first underwent a capacity review, and only afterward moved into actual handling. The gap it left is specific: find the most recent actual invocation of literal default help, and add back how it was invoked and the result the user saw.

This gap cannot be filled with implementation-side declarations. Declarations can explain what settings are present around a parameter, but they cannot serve as evidence of the help page the user saw, nor can they establish whether a prompt occurred during an invocation. If only the original help-page text is obtained, complete the display-layer materials; if only runtime output is obtained, complete the runtime-layer materials. When either side is missing, do not fabricate the other.

By this point, the earlier approach of "look at the result first, then guess the source" has clearly ceased to be valid. It tends to recur because defaults, prompted input, and command-line input can produce the same literal value. Unless the input process was preserved at the time, the final string is insufficient to determine the source.

## Current entry point for investigation

When a report comes in now, do not start by writing "incorrect default source." First record what was observed: a literal default on the help page, `value` after execution, or both. Then collect material according to the branches below.

```text
Report received
├─ Help page only
│  ├─ Save the full original help text
│  ├─ Check the parameter declaration in src/click/core.py
│  ├─ If default is seen: record its presence; do not infer the runtime source
│  ├─ If default_map is seen: record the mapping and displayed text
│  └─ If neither is seen: stop at the display layer and wait for an actual invocation
├─ Runtime result only
│  ├─ First check whether a prompt occurred
│  ├─ Then check the position of explicit command-line input
│  ├─ Save the final value
│  └─ If the input process is missing: leave the source unconfirmed
└─ Both help and runtime results
   ├─ First complete the display-layer material
   ├─ Then complete the runtime-layer material
   └─ Do not merge them prematurely just because the literal values match
```

### A. A literal default appears on the help page

Save the full help output, then find the corresponding parameter declaration. `default` and `default_map` must be recorded separately; do not just write "a default is configured." If the text on the help page matches either one, that only means the display can be checked against the declaration, not that it was used at runtime.

If no default-related settings are found in the declaration, keep the original help text, the parameter location, and the current environment conditions, and stop at the display layer. Whether the directory was set up in advance can be included in the environment conditions, but must not be written down as the cause. Without an actual invocation, do not fill in `value`, a prompt, or command-line input.

### B. The runtime value does not match the expected source

First check whether a prompt occurred in this invocation. If it did, the state before the prompt, the user input, and the final `value` must be kept in the same record. Then check for explicit command-line input and save its original position. Only when both types of input are absent or cannot be recovered should you look back at the default-related settings in the parameter declaration, and record them only as candidates.

A normal help page does not mean the runtime source is normal. Conversely, a runtime value that meets expectations does not prove that the help display is correct. The two windows observe different things and cannot share a single "resolved" status.

### C. Both phenomena occur

First combine the help output and declaration into display material, then combine the input process and final result into runtime material. Being able to check the display layer against the declaration only means there is readable evidence for the help issue; it does not establish a conclusion about the runtime source. Only when the runtime layer includes a prompt or a command-line position can you continue distinguishing between input entry points.

If one window is missing material, retain what has already been confirmed in the other window. Do not compress "the help text and final value are the same" into "the default value caused the anomaly." This is exactly where the old approach stopped prematurely.

## Current source assessment

After the gaps left by the earlier old notes, directory remarks, failure backtracking, window split, and two cards, source attribution should use the category retained by the parameter source object, rather than whether the final strings are identical:

ParameterSource is an enum with stable DEFAULT and DEFAULT_MAP members, and a value supplied by a prompt remains distinguishable from a default or an explicit command-line value.

This requirement can only be applied to a concrete determination when the corresponding source information has already been retained in the actual environment. It does not automatically make old reports distinguishable when they lack prompt records, command-line positions, or actual invocations. When source information is visible, record the actual distinction; when source information has not been retained, state that it is unconfirmed, and retain whatever original help text, declarations, input fragments, or final results have already been obtained.

## Issues not yet split off

An uninitialized state directory remains a related issue. The existing records only require noting, during the next actual invocation, whether the directory was initialized in advance, whether a prompt appeared, the help output the user saw, and the final result; they do not confirm that it changes literal default help, nor do they confirm that it changes the parameter source. When this condition occurs, simply add an observation from the actual environment; do not fold it back into default-value attribution.

Help text width, short help, and formatting differences are not covered on this page. If the same report also includes display issues of this kind, retain the raw output and then move to DOC-13. This page remains responsible for separating parameter source from literal default help, so the two pages do not each repeat the same source determination.

## Old appendix: quick checklist at hand

```text
[Old usage, deprecated]
- Copy the default text from the help page
- Compare it with the final value
- Stop if the two are identical
```

These three lines have not been deleted because old references may still point to them. They explain why the early records reached closure too soon; they are not the current procedure. The current minimum recording requirements are now: for help-page issues, retain the complete original text and parameter declarations; for runtime issues, retain the input entry point and final result; when sources cannot be distinguished, explicitly stop in the corresponding window.

# Help Width and Default Value Migration Notes

This page preserves the migration trail for two old issue names. Both point to `src/click/core.py`: one concerns `help width and defaults`, and the other concerns `short help and formatter width`. Early records grouped the issue names, terminal line wrapping, and display defaults together; that made it quicker to find `parameter`, `help`, `width`, and `defaults`, but conflated three different output sources into a single change.

The old entry point is still useful because it preserves the report's original wording. When tracing back, first lock down the original input, original help output, and old path, then inspect `value`, `default`, `default_map`, `formatter`, `size`, and `columns` within the local scope. The file header shows direct dependencies such as `errno`, `inspect`, `os`, and `sys`; they only help locate things in the file, and the old records did not interpret these imports as a division of responsibility for help rendering.

## Retained Old Flow

The following flow comes from an earlier review. It is retained so we can reproduce why the issues were grouped together at the time:

```text
Help sample from the report
  -> near the parameter of src/click/core.py
     -> default and value
     -> formatter and terminal size
     -> first line of the output
```

The last step is no longer suitable as the sole comparison point for a short description. Samples that happen not to wrap can hide paragraph boundaries when only the first line is taken; on a narrow terminal, a change to the first line may also be nothing more than a layout effect. The old notes also recorded "the default value text did not change" as supporting evidence that the formatter did not change. That judgment is no longer used. It is retained because some old reports are still named along this path; that does not mean it can determine current behavior.

## Migration Record by Difference

When moving from old examples to comparable records, do not rewrite the output first. Each sample should answer only one question.

**Displayed default.** Save the parameter input and the complete help text. First confirm that the comparison is of the final displayed default, not some local `value`. Then trace the parameter-related locations to check whether `default_map` contributes to this display. If all you can see is one property layer or an adjacent code block, record only the object observed; do not generalize a local result into a migration rule for all parameters.

**Format width.** Save the runtime terminal environment and untruncated output, then inspect `size`, `columns`, and `formatter`. Width changes usually appear as different line-wrap positions, but wrapping by itself cannot prove that default-value calculation changed. To compare with an old sample, retain the complete paragraphs in both outputs rather than only the line that looks visually closest.

**Short description.** Record the first paragraph of the help text, then observe how it is presented at the given width. This separates the source of the summary text from the formatter's line-wrapping result. The "first line of the output" in the old flow can still be used to locate a report quickly, but it cannot replace this paragraph record.

The recently added counterexample is at the test entry for CLK-204: it requires adding a repository test from the user example in `help width and defaults` and saving the current failure text or output bytes. The CLK-221 entry retains the direct trigger for `short help and formatter width` and requires saving the input and the tool's actual output. The two cards are for locating the relevant material; this page does not treat their subsequent status as part of the old report.

## Later Local Clarification

The old records did not distinguish the three outcomes. After subsequent verification, the fixed description for this area is:

Help rendering uses a default_map value when calculating a displayed default, reads the terminal-size columns attribute for formatter width, and derives a short help summary from the first paragraph.

This correction addresses only these three points in help rendering. It does not endorse all the formatter speculation in the old notes, nor does it explain how each caller should change. When new output differs from an old sample, first identify whether the difference concerns the default, width, or short description; if one output contains two kinds of changes, still save them separately under the three objects.

## Restoring the Old Path

When the new entry has no comparable result, keep the recovery sequence simple: retrieve the original help input, retrieve the output saved at the time, return to the old location in `src/click/core.py`, and then add the new direct-trigger result. Do not substitute text produced with a different terminal column count, a manually removed default, or a reassembled first line for the missing sample.

This record is still suitable for starting a local check from an old issue name. It does not cover every detail of help formatting; the merged judgment in the old path should not be treated as the current troubleshooting conclusion.

# Decision Record for Completion Environment Dispatch and Echo

The final decision retained on this page is not to find one overarching explanation for completion and terminal output, but to maintain the two tracks separately. completion environment dispatch requires following local references to confirm how the environment, variables, and protocol connect to command execution; prompt echo ordering requires reproducible output samples. The two can cross-reference each other, but cannot borrow each other's conclusions.

## The Initial Split That Was Retained

The early view seemed straightforward: since both issues were included in the wrap-up scope of completion-and-terminal-2026.07, environment variable handling might explain the echo after a command completes. This view was not retained as a decision. It mixed two different subjects of observation and mistook "we can start reading near the file" for "we already know the call order."

Two ways of recording this were actually compared at the time.

| Approach | What it provides | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Combine them into one explanation of normal command execution | A shorter page that readers can read through from a single entry point | A mistaken conclusion about completion would also contaminate the conclusion about echo ordering, and it would remain unclear which path the variables actually serve |
| Keep two separate documentation tracks | Each waits for its own local evidence, making the effects of changes easier to examine separately | The page will not immediately provide a unified conclusion about terminal behavior |

The second approach was adopted. The decision concerns how to document and verify behavior, not the addition of another implementation. The completion track first confirms the local relationships between environment, variable, protocol, and command execution; the echo track first preserves the observed order before, during, and after completion. Similar names were not pieced together into an unverified execution chain.

## How One Track Became Two

The initial draft only said that both the "completion environment" and "unstable echo" needed additional records. Later, when the entry points were reviewed again, it became clear that the two needed different evidence: the former could be investigated further through environment- and protocol-related references within `src/click/core.py`, while the latter first required actual command samples to determine exactly where the output seen by users occurred.

The completion record therefore retained the narrow scope supported by the file itself. The direct dependencies visible at the top of the file are:

```text
import errno
import inspect
import os
import sys
```

These imports show that this is a suitable local entry point, but they are not dispatch rules. What still needs to be examined is the declarations and references adjacent to environment, variable, protocol, command, and execution within the file. Imports alone cannot determine whether an environment variable serves only completion or also affects normal command execution; a filename alone cannot substitute for call order either.

The echo record, meanwhile, did not treat help text as a behavioral result. The observation recorded when `CLK-223` was created was "prompt echo ordering output cannot be reproduced reliably," and the entry point provided by the card was to execute commands as written in the help text and observe what users could still see after the commands completed. Help text is useful for guiding reproduction, but is not enough on its own to settle output ordering. Without actual samples, neither "echo always occurs after completion ends" nor "all commands echo in the same order" can be adopted as the current position.

## Timeline of the Work

`CLK-206` appeared first. It addressed missing runtime records for the completion environment and asked the corresponding module maintainer to check current behavior and identify an entry point for further investigation. Work began on month 9, day 17, and review was requested on month 9, day 22. What can be confirmed here is the gap in the records and the direction for rechecking; the card's request cannot directly supply a complete runtime chain.

The issue in `CLK-223` was later pursued separately. Work began on month 10, day 29, and became blocked on month 11, day 13, with the specific reason recorded as waiting for upstream to provide samples that could be shared publicly. This blocker does not mean that echo ordering has stabilized, nor does it mean that the completion track needs to pause; it only means that the echo track lacks input for further comparison.

These two periods were not merged into a single incident. `CLK-206` concerns the verification entry point for completion environment dispatch, while `CLK-223` concerns the reproduction gap for prompt echo ordering. They appear on the same page because the requirements history placed them in adjacent wrap-up scopes, not because evidence already proves that one phenomenon caused the other.

A narrower reminder was also retained during review: both the issue name and the call name can lead people to `src/click/core.py`, but this only determines where to start looking. It does not establish that the environment variables near that path constitute the entirety of completion behavior, nor that the output order recorded there covers all normal command execution. This reminder was not removed because the same misreading could still occur when the file is investigated again later.

## Boundaries of the Verification Entry Points

When investigating completion, start with the environment and protocol relationships in `src/click/core.py`, then look back at references near command execution. What needs to be recorded is the local relationships: where environment selection occurs, how variables enter protocol-related branches, and whether those branches subsequently connect to the area around command execution. If a step appears only at the top of the file or in a declaration, stop there rather than expanding an import into caller behavior.

When investigating echo, first preserve the original output order in the sample, then mark whether it occurs before, during, or after completion. If the order changes across repeated runs, preserve the change itself; if it cannot be reproduced, it can only be recorded as not reliably reproducible. Do not choose an explanation first and then fill in the intermediate steps using similar call names.

This is also the division of responsibility between the two tracks. The `click-core` side confirms the local relationships and completion entry point within `src/click/core.py`; `CLK-206` provides navigation to the missing environment records. The echo side needs samples and the observed order; `CLK-223` provides the reproduction entry point and its subsequent gaps. If an interface review involves the shell-first callback name or path object conversion, go to `DOC-16`; this page does not re-establish interface decisions.

Compatibility impacts are also examined separately. If the completion entry point changes, first confirm whether the change affects only completion dispatch or also reaches normal command execution. If echo ordering changes, first confirm whether the change occurs before, during, or after command completion, then compare where the output of existing commands appears. Neither item has finalized change commands, version numbers, or result samples, so no rollback step is invented here.

## Relationships Retained in the Diagram

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> split
    state "Split into two documentation tracks" as split
    state "completion environment verification" as completion
    state "prompt echo reproduction" as echo
    state "Check against local references" as local_check
    state "Wait for publicly shareable samples" as waiting_sample
    split --> completion
    split --> echo
    completion --> local_check
    echo --> waiting_sample
```

The diagram does not merge the two tracks into one completed state. The completion track can currently continue checking local references; the echo track remains at the point where samples are insufficient. The two cards each point to their own entry point, and `DOC-16` serves only as navigation to adjacent interface material.

## Decisions Currently Available for Use

Three points remain usable. First, `src/click/core.py` is the verification entry point for completion environment dispatch. Second, prompt echo ordering cannot be settled directly from help text and must await actual observations. Third, any change must be assessed separately for its impact on completion dispatch and normal command execution; the two cannot share a single compatibility assessment simply because they both appear in the terminal wrap-up context.

What remains unresolved is not the page format, but two specific facts: whether there are broader effects between the completion entry point and all normal command execution; and, in reproducible samples, the order of output users actually see before and after command completion. The latter remains unconfirmed until upstream supplies public samples. If new material concerns only one track, update only the corresponding section, preserving the other track's original record and the rationale for the split.

Related entry points: `CLK-206`, `CLK-223`. For adjacent decisions on interface names and path object conversion, see `DOC-16`.

# Callback Naming and Path Conversion Proposal

This proposal originally aimed only to check whether the naming was adequate. We later found that names and object forms need to be considered separately. The discussion remains focused on `src/click/core.py`: it exposes the completion-related entry points and their adjacent dependencies, but that does not make this file responsible for all conversions. The experiment compares only local state before and after the call; it does not redefine the entire completion flow.

The options that retain the shell-first entry point are:

- Keep requests originating from the generated Bash completion source, retain `_CLI_COMPLETE=` for environment selection, and use `_CLI_COMPLETE=<owner-confirmed callback instruction>` for the actual call.
- The `Command` side still receives these requests through `_main_shell_completion`. Keep `<owner-confirmed generated response declaration>` inside the callback function to collect the response first, then pass it to the existing output path.
- Candidates without descriptions still go out in the existing observable format, for example `<owner-confirmed undescribed candidate wire format>`. Do not tie this to path object conversion yet; otherwise, a single failure will not tell us whether the problem is naming, dispatch, or encoding.

There are two possible points for path object conversion. The first is before entering the shell-first callback. This gives the callback stable input and requires fewer caller changes. However, if the original caller needs information on the path object, the conversion happens too early, and rollback must restore the object form before the entry point. The second is after the callback has produced the completion candidates. This lets the callback retain the original input and is useful for first observing how the object changes during completion. The cost is that the output layer must explicitly distinguish values that are already text from those that are still path objects; a single string comparison cannot replace that check.

The earlier draft placed "successful call" next to "callback naming is usable" and reached a conclusion too quickly. A counterexample was later recorded in [CLK-207], showing that failed calls need to be retained alongside the successful path. That record does not provide a unified implementation decision that can be directly generalized, so it is not treated here as proof of a pass. Another check is available at [CLK-224]: reproduce path object conversion starting from the pre-call state, and observe whether any additional visible changes remain after completion. The two cards serve as a counterexample and a before-and-after state comparison, respectively; they are not combined into a generalized checklist.

Use this review order to start:

1. Change only the shell-first callback name, leave path objects unchanged, and record the visible output for both success and failure.
2. Revert the name change, move only the path object conversion point, and record the objects received by the callback and the candidate values after completion.

The original May judgment was that candidate encoding and deprecation display are both things users see in the terminal, so they could first be handled in one verification pass. Whether the candidate line format can be preserved consistently should be observed from the existing test entry; whether the deprecation display actually appears depends on the invocation used in the latest report and the result seen by the user. This was intended to avoid treating a file pointed to by the issue name as the common endpoint for two phenomena.

The original draft gave too much weight to the fact that they "look adjacent in the terminal." In May, there was no related ticket that could be cited, so the original draft did not provide a task ID or investigation entry point.

The two items were subsequently connected to existing work entries separately. CLK-211 cover only the candidate wire check: run candidate wire encoding through the existing test entry and retain the affected units together with adjacent unchanged units. The point is not to describe all completion behavior again, but to keep units that did not change alongside the encoding changes so the scope of impact is visible.

The direction of CLK-228 is different. It requires finding the real invocation from the latest report of deprecation display, then restoring the invocation method and the result seen by the user. The earlier claim that the "terminal text is adjacent" cannot replace this step: the candidate options may come from the test entry, while deprecation display has a comparable object only after returning to the invocation described in the report. The review still did not merge the two sets of material into one display conclusion.

    Verify Separately --> Display Invocation Investigation: CLK-228
    Candidate Encoding Review --> Retain Adjacent Units

The decision is to maintain two independent verification entry points. This old judgment is retained so that people following old links understand why this page contains two topics at once.
