# Partial Shell Token Parsing Troubleshooting Tree

This page starts with a narrowly scoped case: the actual entry point for a partial shell token produces results that differ from those saved in the example. The troubleshooting goal is to isolate the difference at an observable stage, not to attribute all completion behavior to `src/click/core.py`. The same set of reproduction materials must show the input tokens, actual output, runtime version, and entry point used together; if any item is missing, record only up to that gap.

## Preserve the Case This Way First

Do not trim tokens first, and do not remove blank lines, empty strings, or empty `argument` from the output. Save the original input and the content returned by the tool first, then write a separate explanation for readability. If the example has been manually formatted, it must be placed alongside the original result; otherwise, "entry point mismatch" and "presentation mismatch" will get mixed together.

The input must not be described merely as "some partial token" either. Preserve the order and boundaries of the tokens, especially the last, still-incomplete part. Text that looks identical may give the parser different input if its leading or trailing whitespace, empty strings, or token segmentation differs. Do not clean up the input first here; a cleaned-up copy can serve as a comparison, but it cannot replace the original materials.

Save the output in two layers as well: what the tool actually returned, and how it was formatted for readability. Record the absence of a callback result separately from a callback returning an empty result. The former does not yet prove that the parsing entry point was entered; the latter is already a return, and the empty content itself is still an observation.

## Decision Tree

```text
partial shell token
    ├─ Entry point not triggered
    │    ├─ Input is not the same set of tokens
    │    │    └─ Stop at input comparison, retain both sets of materials
    │    └─ Input is the same but there is no callback result
    │         └─ Stop at entry point verification, do not explain the parser
    ├─ Entry point triggered, result differs from the example
    │    ├─ Token boundaries differ
    │    │    └─ Compare token shapes before and after parsing
    │    ├─ Argument order differs
    │    │    └─ Preserve the actual order, then check the branch location
    │    └─ Extra empty argument
    │         └─ Check whether it appeared during splitting or was added later
    └─ Entry point triggered, result is the same
         └─ Stop at this example, do not expand into other completion issues
```

The stopping points in this tree are important. If the entry point was not triggered, continuing to discuss the parser merely describes a path that never ran as though it had run. If the entry point was triggered but the tokens differ, the difference still cannot be attributed directly to the implementation. Only after the input, entry point, and output have been aligned is it meaningful to compare the subsequent completion branches.

### Entry Point Not Triggered

First verify the entry point name used in the reproduction materials, then verify whether the token is still in a partial state. If the name comes from an old example, do not assume the two calls are the same just because it resembles the current name. Also confirm whether the output comes from the same run; a screenshot, copied results, and input from another run must not be stitched into a single record.

If the entry point names really differ, label the old example as using the old entry point and stop troubleshooting here. At this point, `src/click/core.py` can be retained as a path for tracing back, but the path itself must not be treated as evidence that the entry point executed. The only direct dependencies currently visible at the top of the file are `errno`, `inspect`, `os`, and `sys`; these names only indicate local file adjacency, not that they explain this difference.

If the entry point name is the same but there is no callback result, still stop at the entry point layer first. Record the fact that there is no result and retain the tokens passed in; do not fill the gap with an expected completion output. If the raw return from the same entry point becomes available later, compare the new materials and the old example side by side.

### Entry Point Triggered but Result Differs

Put the tokens before parsing and the `argument` after parsing into two columns. First compare token boundaries and order, then compare the arrangement and count of `argument` and the position where an empty value first appears. Do not collapse these differences into "parsing error," because an extra empty `argument` may appear during splitting or be added in a later branch, and these require different troubleshooting entry points.

If the result differs only because line breaks or markers were changed for presentation, preserve the tool's raw output and attach the formatted version separately. Do not judge what the parser returned based on the formatted text. If the example itself retains only formatted text, record this gap rather than inferring the missing tokens.

If the difference disappears after changing environments, record only the runtime version and environment differences, and treat that result as a failure to reproduce in another environment. Environment differences can change the observation conditions, but cannot by themselves prove that the source code has been fixed. Only if the same environment still consistently produces the same difference should you continue tracing back through the local declarations in `src/click/core.py` adjacent to `token`, `parsing`, `parser`, and `argument`.

One recovery action can easily be misleading: deleting the trailing empty `argument` first, or completing the partial token into a full token, to make the examples look consistent. This changes the input under investigation and cannot count as a fix. You can create a separate comparison using a full token, but the two results can only show that the inputs differ, not that the parser is now handling them correctly.

### Output Matches

When the input, entry point, and output all match, stop at this example. Do not extend it to other argument behavior just to make it cover another completion use case. Recording a match only means that this case did not reproduce the difference; it does not mean that the old example's mismatch has been explained. If the old example still lacks a runtime version or raw output, retain those gaps in the record.

## Changes in the Assessment

Early records described the issue as "possibly pointing to the wrong entry point." At the time, the only available information was the trace-back path `src/click/core.py` and the four direct dependencies at the top of the file: `errno`, `inspect`, `os`, and `sys`. This working hypothesis can guide the next step, but without a comparison of the input, entry point, and raw output, it cannot be treated as the root cause.

Subsequent review narrowed the assessment to: first distinguish whether the entry point was triggered, then compare token shapes and the arrangement of `argument`. The old "wrong entry point" assessment remains in the historical section because it really was the hypothesis at the time; the correction is that troubleshooting must not end solely on an entry point name difference, and a path name must not be treated as evidence of a call. Until the same input, same entry point, and same runtime version have all been fully aligned, the root cause remains unconfirmed.

## Review Entry Point and Recording Order

Start tracing back from `src/click/core.py`, looking only at the local declarations adjacent to the token, parsing, parser, and `argument` involved in this case. Keep each comparison in a single record in the following order:

- The entry point name used, and whether it was actually entered;
- The original boundaries and order of the partial tokens;
- Token shapes before and after parsing;
- The order and count of `argument`, and when empty values appear;
- The tool's raw output and the example output;
- The runtime version and visible environment differences.

If the first item differs, stop at the entry point layer; if the second differs, first fix the comparison of the reproduction materials; if the boundaries are the same but `argument` differs, preserve both shapes and locate where the difference first appears. Only after that first location is clear is it worth continuing to inspect the subsequent completion branches. Do not add unconfirmed callers or dependencies to this path.

## Case Links

CLK-213 serves only as navigation for this case: it records that the actual entry point for a partial shell token produces results that differ from the example. Historical actions on the card cannot replace the input and output, nor can they supply this page with a run that was never saved. When reviewing, return from the card to this page, first check whether the original materials are complete, then choose a branch of the decision tree.

If the same input consistently produces the same result in the current environment, the location of the difference can be referred back to the local path in `src/click/core.py`; if the result changes with the version or environment, preserve the differences first rather than attributing environment-related behavior to the parsing implementation; if it cannot be triggered again, troubleshooting only needs to reach the entry point or reproduction-materials layer, and the old example is still worth keeping.

### Old Examples Still Retained

- The old example gives one name for the entry point, but the actual reproduction materials do not prove that the two are the same.
- The empty `argument` in the old example was once treated as noise that could be cleaned up; that handling approach has been abandoned, while the original example is still retained.
- Completing tokens to obtain the "expected result" is no longer used either, because it changes the input under investigation.

These old examples should not be copied into new expected results. All that can currently be confirmed is: the input, entry point, token shapes, and actual output must be compared together; any missing item should cause troubleshooting to stop at the corresponding branch.

# Prompt Callback Recovery Decision Record

The initial issue was not whether to retain the prompt, but which part should continue evaluating the value after the callback provided input; when the result was not accepted, where responsibility for asking again should reside. The only local entry point established at the time was `src/click/core.py`. The file header showed direct imports of `errno`, `inspect`, `os`, and `sys`, but these dependencies were not enough to show that recovery already had an independent layer.

Three placement options were compared. The first would have the callback handle recovery itself; it is closest to the input, but would force the callback to deal with the option, value, error text, and asking again. The second would keep the callback on the input side, with prompt validation handling results that were not accepted. The third would add a recovery entry point outside the command, rewrap the failure, and return it to the prompt.

The second option is the tentative choice. The callback should not thereby acquire a command-level lifecycle, nor should every callback repeatedly handle `BadParameter` and `message`. Do not add a new entry point outside the command at this stage, because it would introduce another acceptance condition and make it difficult to determine later who decided to stop or continue.

This decision fixes responsibility, but not the return path. Where the value of `prompted` returns after a failure for the next prompt, and whether it still carries the original option state, have not been confirmed. Retain the existing prompt validation boundary; if local references show the same recovery action repeated in multiple places, then discuss whether to extract a helper.

# Prompt Callback Recovery Decision Record

Early notes placed prompt callback recovery on the prompt validation side. That wording only settled the boundary at the time: the callback provides input, while the option and command retain the decisions about the value, error handling, and re-prompting. It did not answer which local object the input re-enters the prompt through after a failure, nor confirm whether the callback is called again.

The review still started by examining the objects adjacent to `src/click/core.py`. The lookup terms visible here include prompt, callback, option, prompted, value, before, command, BadParameter, message, until, and accepted. They indicate that the recovery problem spans input, validation, and the termination condition; they cannot form a complete call graph on their own. For that reason, this review did not add a new helper, return type, or caller based on the names, and did not interpret the `errno`, `inspect`, `os`, and `sys` in the file header as new dispatch relationships.

## Placement Options Compared at the Time

Having the callback recover on its own appears to keep input and retry together, but in practice it pushes the outer semantics into every callback. The callback would need to know why a value was not accepted, where the error should be shown, and whether the next prompt should still use the same option. Even if an old callback could continue returning values, it should not be forced to understand the command's termination condition. In particular, if the relationship between `BadParameter` and `message` is handled by both the callback and validation, the error text could appear twice.

Adding a recovery layer outside the command was also rejected. This approach could wrap a failure as a unified event, but it would duplicate the existing decision logic. `before`, `until`, and accepted all concern whether to continue or stop; when they fall in validation and the outer command layer respectively, it becomes difficult to determine which location actually made the decision, even if the same symptom is observed later. The available material does not show a need for a new public command-level entry point, so "unification" is not used as a reason to add one.

Preserving the prompt validation boundary has a lower cost. The callback can continue to provide only input, while validation continues to handle the option, value, and error paths. "Preserving" here does not mean that validation already has a verified recovery loop; it means that a rejected result should not first be pushed down to the callback or moved outside the command. Stabilizing responsibilities before call details keeps the next review from changing both boundaries at once.

## Correction After Review

The public record for CLK-216 added a correction during the review: in the `Prompt validation` section, prompt callback recovery still has one unconfirmed point. This invalidated the convenient implication in the early notes—locating it at validation does not mean that the callback's return path is known.

Two judgments are therefore kept separate. The first can serve as the decision: do not add a command-level recovery entry point, do not require the callback to understand the command's error loop, and have prompt validation continue to own the boundary for acceptance decisions and error handling. The second remains an open question: after a failure, is the next input obtained by the same validation block, or does execution return to the earlier prompt call site; if input is obtained again, is the option context from the first attempt reused?

Extracting a recovery helper inside validation immediately was considered. The advantage is that the destination after a failure could later be checked independently; the drawback is that it would establish a responsibility name before the input and output had been verified. Keeping the existing local path lets readers continue checking the flow in the same section, but it does not use a seemingly stable interface to conceal the unconfirmed point. The latter is the choice at this stage. If it is later confirmed that the same recovery action is used in multiple places, extraction can be reconsidered; until then, extracting a helper is not the fix itself.

When reviewing this issue next, first confirm where the failure object is formed, then confirm whether the object that re-prompts still holds the original option. If the symptom is duplicated error text, first check whether the generation and consumption of `BadParameter` and `message` occur at the same boundary; if the symptom is that the input does not appear again, first check whether `prompted` has already been judged non-accepted. The two symptoms may be adjacent, but they cannot share an unconfirmed attribution. CLK-216 is retained as the navigation for this review.

# Prompt Callback Recovery Decision Record

This record preserves a narrow decision: prompt callback recovery remains within the existing prompt validation boundary. No separate command-level recovery entry point will be created, and responsibility for recovery will not be pushed down to each callback. The decision addresses responsibility assignment; it does not assume that all call details have already been investigated.

The initial problem was small. The prompt had already obtained input, and the callback also participated in processing that input; when the result was not accepted, the system still had to decide whether to prompt again. At the time, it was easy to treat "prompt again" as an internal callback action because the callback was closest to the input. Looking back later revealed that input being close to the callback does not mean that the acceptance conditions, error text, and termination conditions should also be owned by the callback.

The local verification entry point has consistently been `src/click/core.py`. The file header directly imports:

```python
import errno
import inspect
import os
import sys
```

These items are retained in this record to show the scope of the investigation at the time, not to establish an additional module boundary for recovery. The early investigation went from the issue names for prompt, callback, and option to this file; an import list or file location alone cannot establish a complete call graph.

## Tradeoffs left by the initial draft

The initial draft compared three possible placements.

The first was to let the callback recover on its own. This keeps value retrieval and retry in the same place and looks direct, but the callback would need to know why an input was not accepted and choose when to prompt again. This would expose the callback to state that originally belonged to option, value, and command. Even if an old callback could still return a value, it would be forced to understand how failure is handled.

The second was to have prompt validation handle recovery. The callback would only provide input, and the returned value would still go through the existing acceptance check; when it was not accepted, this boundary would decide whether to continue prompting. This would not require the callback to add recovery parameters or expose the command lifecycle to the callback. The initial draft provisionally adopted this option.

The third was to add a recovery entry point outside command. This approach attempted to wrap failures uniformly, at the cost of duplicating the check outside the original boundary. `before`, `until`, and accepted all appeared in the review context at the time; if they were interpreted separately in two places, the timing of stopping and continuing might no longer be consistent. The initial draft did not identify which existing check the new entry point would have to replace, so it was not adopted.

The shortcomings of the initial draft should also be retained. It said that "validation handles recovery" but did not clearly distinguish responsibility from control flow. The initial draft did not pin down where the value of `prompted` returns to the next prompt after validation fails, or whether it remains in the original option context. That version can serve as the source of the boundary decision, but it cannot be treated as a completed call graph.

## Later review separated the questions

The subsequent review did not overturn the second tradeoff; it split it into two questions.

The first question is responsibility: who decides that an input is accepted, and who handles a result that is not accepted. The original judgment still stands. The callback does not handle command-level recovery; no second, duplicate entry point is added outside command; prompt validation remains the boundary for checking acceptance conditions and handling errors.

The second question is control flow: after a failure, which local object gives the next input back to the prompt. This cannot be brushed aside by saying that "everything is in validation." A boundary can be responsible for making a decision without that proving that it owns the complete loop; conversely, an unconfirmed loop does not mean that responsibility should be redistributed to the callback or the outer command layer.

The review scope still covers only the local neighborhood of `src/click/core.py`. Visible terms include prompt, callback, option, prompted, value, before, command, BadParameter, message, until, and accepted. They are sufficient to support the discussion of boundaries and compatibility costs in this decision, but insufficient to determine from their names alone any unseen helper, caller, or returned object. Previously, someone casually treated "a term appears in the same file" as "it is passed by the same function"; that assumption was not carried forward this time.

At this stage, extracting the recovery action inside validation into a helper was considered again. The benefit would be that the return-flow conditions could later be checked independently, and the burden of reading the same logic could be reduced. The problem is that the helper's inputs and outputs are not yet stable: it is not known exactly where the input is obtained again after failure, nor whether the option context is preserved unchanged. Naming it first would make an unverified relationship look like a stable interface.

Therefore, the current choice is not to extract a new helper. This does not mean that a helper will never be needed; it means that, for now, we should avoid adding a local object whose responsibility has not been verified. If it is later confirmed that the same recovery action is genuinely reused in multiple places, extraction can be evaluated according to the call relationships at that time; it must not be extracted first and then treated as evidence that recovery has already been completed.

## Correction in the review record

The review record for CLK-216 retains one correction: in the `Prompt validation` section, one part of prompt callback recovery remains unconfirmed. This correction addresses the excessive closure of the earlier draft, not the boundary status of validation.

What must be withdrawn is a stronger implication: once validation has been located, we already know how the callback flows back. The existing material does not support that claim. What must be retained is the weaker but actionable decision: the callback is not responsible for command-level recovery, no recovery entry point is duplicated outside command, and validation continues to handle acceptance checks and error handling.

These two layers of information cannot be combined into one sentence. If unconfirmed control flow is written as established behavior, subsequent investigation will focus only on the callback and overlook where the failure object is formed. If the boundary check is removed because the control flow is unclear, we will return to the approach in which multiple callers handle errors independently. The current record retains the boundary while explicitly leaving the path unknown.

The state diagram below describes only the stages distinguished by this decision. The final state is not an implementation conclusion, but the destination for further investigation.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Callback
    Callback: callback returns input
    Callback --> Validation
    Validation: prompt validation
    Validation --> Accepted: accepted
    Validation --> Pending: Not accepted
    Pending: destination after failure pending investigation
    Pending --> [*]
```

The diagram does not draw an arrow from the pending-investigation state back to callback or prompt. The current material cannot yet confirm whether recovery occurs within the same validation loop or returns to an earlier prompt call site. Drawing either arrow as fact would exceed the scope of what this decision establishes.

## Compatibility is why there is no external entry point

Compatibility with old callbacks is an important reason to retain the boundary. If the callback only provides input, existing users do not need to add recovery parameters or understand the command's termination conditions. If the callback starts identifying failure reasons, it must understand the relationship between `BadParameter` and `message`; semantics originally handled on the validation side would then leak into callback implementations.

Error text is a concrete risk. If the callback discovers that a value is unsuitable and displays `message` once on its own, while validation displays it once again based on the same failure, the caller sees a duplicate error. Conversely, if the callback does nothing because it does not know where the error originated, it cannot independently guarantee when to prompt again. Keeping the callback responsible for input avoids separately guessing the error-handling rules in two places.

The value lifecycle also cannot be simplified to "the callback returns, and the prompt ends." `value` still has to go through the option's acceptance check and may have an ordering relationship with the result of `prompted`. This page does not describe that ordering as a verified call graph; the currently available verification direction is to first inspect which layer generates the failure result, and then inspect whether the next prompt still uses the original option state.

`before` and `until` likewise cannot be moved to the command layer prematurely. They were used as terms related to termination conditions in the earlier review, but this page has no evidence showing which loop each one controls. If recovery is modified later, first confirm their actual relationship with accepted, then decide whether to correct the existing path or extract a local helper. Copying the conditions first and then using the result to explain duplicated behavior is not an acceptable change sequence.

## Current reading order

When prompt behavior needs to be changed, start by reading the code adjacent to prompt validation, callback, option, and value in `src/click/core.py`. First confirm the failure object, then confirm the object that prompts again, and only afterward discuss whether a new API name is needed. The file path here is a verification entry point; this decision does not include the rest of the Click runtime, such as completion, terminal, or other flows.

If the symptom is duplicated error text, first check the producers and consumption sites of `BadParameter` and `message`. Do not first make the callback print the error again on the assumption that this will supplement validation's information.

If the symptom is that the input does not appear again, first check whether the value of `prompted` has already been determined to be non-accepted, and then check whether validation still holds the original option context. This symptom and duplicated error text may occur near the same part of the flow, but they are not the same failure description and must not be assigned the same cause by default.

If a caller requests a new recovery hook, first state which existing check that hook will replace. Without a replacement target, adding an entry point outside command will only coexist with validation and cannot explain which of the two owns the termination conditions. The implementation details of adjacent integration work are not in this local material, so they cannot be written here as a commitment made by click-core.

CLK-216 are retained as review entry points for prompt callback recovery, focusing on whether the relevant paths are created when there is no old cache or personal configuration. They help return to the verification context at the time and do not replace this page's distinction between responsibility and control flow. DOC-26 discuss confirmation interaction; both involve interaction, but neither carries this page's recovery decision.

## Objects still requiring verification

- Whether the next prompt after a failure continues in the same validation loop or returns to an earlier prompt call site.
- Whether the callback executes again during recovery; if so, whether the option, command, and value passed in are the same as the first time.
- Whether the producer and final presenter of `message` are the same local object.
- The actual short-circuit order of `before`, `until`, and accepted.
- Whether there is a sufficiently stable recovery action that is genuinely reused often enough to justify extracting it into a helper without changing the behavior of old callbacks.

These questions do not reopen the current decision. They show that implementation verification is not complete. If new code fragments or test output become available later, they should be added beside the corresponding question; if the results overturn the judgment that validation owns the boundary, the correction must be stated explicitly rather than continuing to use the initial draft's provisional wording.

| Scenario | Observation to record first | What cannot be concluded directly |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Confirmation with a default value | Whether the default value participates in the result when the response is missing | This does not show that all prompts use the same rule |
| Confirmation without a default value | Whether an empty response triggers another prompt | A repeated prompt does not establish an independent entry point |
| Custom confirmation | Whether custom handling still follows the same convention | It cannot be categorized solely by the text `custom` |
| Default value is `None` | Whether it is distinguished from having no default value | The two cannot be assumed to be equivalent or different |

The "cannot be concluded" column matters. If two results are the same, we still need to record whether they came from the same path or whether different handling happened to produce the same result. The old draft did not preserve this distinction, making it easy to misrecord identical output as an identical entry point. Conversely, if two samples behave differently, we should first confirm which condition—default value, empty response, or custom handling—caused the difference before discussing whether confirmation needs its own handling point.

One actual review also changed the ranking of the candidate options. Previously, "separate confirmation" looked easier for writing regression names; after the review, the real risk became that calls to Fang Ke could lock in a new entry point based on a provisional classification. Continuing to use the existing prompt path makes the sample names less tidy, but it avoids turning the classification into an interface commitment prematurely. Therefore, this round will first record where the default value, empty response, and repeated prompt lead, without introducing new names or changing other prompt paths.

This does not mean confirmation can never be listed separately. If the actual call adjacency shows that confirmation consistently goes through handling outside the general prompt, the separate treatment can be reevaluated; the comparison at that point should be based on existing call relationships and sample results, not on how neat the regression table's naming looks. Similarly, if custom confirmation ultimately reuses the existing handling, the sample can remain as a coverage case without expanding the interface surface for that reason.

CLK-217 is the entry-point investigation card. It requires comparing against the artifacts available in the previous round and updating only the jobs or pinned versions that actually changed. It is cited here only to locate the inspection scope; the card itself cannot replace the judgment about the confirmation interaction. If entry-point changes need to be investigated further from the caller's perspective, go to DOC-27; this record retains only the trade-offs around confirmation semantics and regression samples.

Three items remain unresolved. When an empty response triggers another prompt, who retains the default-value information in the result; whether custom confirmation can bypass the same handling point; and whether samples whose default value is `None` need to enter regression separately. The current material is insufficient to decide these three items.

The withdrawal condition is more specific than in the early version: if further inspection can confirm only that prompt objects exist, while still failing to find a call relationship that consistently separates confirmation from general input, withdraw the trial of an independent handling point and do not turn this proposal into an interface commitment. In that case, retain the sample records and wait for a review based on actual calls and results.

# Caller Integration Exit Window Checklist

This checklist is used in the short window for click-client-integration. It does not determine whether caller integration has been released; it only records the small stretch when the live setup changes from "still in integration" to "ready to exit." The original usage was fairly simple: if the last result was visible, treat the window as closed. That judgment remains here, while the release conclusion is still signed off separately by the relevant owner.

## Record one line when opening the window

- [ ] Find the `docs/adj-click/release/click-client-integration-Exit Window Checklist.md` used for this run; do not start another copy with the same name.
- [ ] In the same place, record the entry point for the actual caller sample and the result when it first became visible. If the sample comes from an example being adapted, leave the example itself beside the record.
- [ ] If this integration run involved switching between the current and old entry points, first check the migration index for DOC-31; in the checklist, record only which side actually exited in this window.

Do not start the window if there is no entry point or no first visible result. If the old sample cannot be recovered, do not substitute another caller's sample; the resulting exit record would mix the two integration boundaries.

## Exit action

1. First complete the exit action agreed for this caller integration, then retrieve the last visible result. Do not paste an earlier green result first and use it as this run's result.
2. Record the exit action and result in the same section. If the result is empty, the entry point has already switched, or the record can only show "ran once," stop closing the window immediately; return to the integration state from before the exit action and continue only after the original sample has been restored.
3. adj-click's exit action must be checked off separately. The caller having stopped trying does not mean the integration side has exited; do not combine the two into one "complete" item.

This earlier convention uses the last visible result as the basis for closing the window, making quick handoffs during a shift easier. It does not include release success, adaptation results from other callers, or later entry-point migration. When you encounter any of these, do not turn this page into a release conclusion; retain only the reason the window remains open.

## What to leave in the handoff

The handoff records only three items: the person handing off, the person taking over, and the confirmation time. Put incomplete items directly after the corresponding exit action; do not replace a name with "the project team will continue to monitor." If the person taking over can confirm only that the caller has stopped, but cannot confirm adj-click's exit action, leave the latter unchecked.

# Caller Integration Testing Route Proposal

This record first captures the route that was not adopted at the time, so integration testing doesn't go back to guessing from old screenshots and scattered examples. The source material is still at `docs/adj-click/proposals/not-adopted-click-caller-integration-testing-route.md`; the sample calls there have not yet been organized into a fixed integration approach.

The choice at the time was narrow: continue with `callback forwarding`, or split out `completion dispatch`. The former appeared to require fewer changes, since callers could keep using the existing callback entry point. The problem was that the callback mixed request handoff with post-completion handling. In the examples, the failure exits for the two parts were different. Adding more branches to the same layer would make it hard for callers to tell which exit still allowed recovery.

The idea behind splitting out `completion dispatch` was not to replace all entry points. It would only handle requests that had already reached the completion stage, then return to the caller based on that stage's result. This would let us try the integration with a set of real sample calls first, without migrating paths that had not yet been checked. The trade-off is that integration testing would temporarily have two views: the old entry point would still treat completion as part of the callback chain, while the new entry point would treat it as an independent dispatch point. If the samples themselves did not expose this distinction, the split would just add another named layer.

The reason for not adopting `callback forwarding` at this stage was not that it had already stopped working. It suits calls with only one failure exit; what remains uncertain is whether all the existing samples fit that case. To avoid mistaking "can forward" for "can recover," the trial would check only two things: whether the original caller could still be identified after the request entered the completion stage, and whether a failure could return to the original entry point. The second check needs a set of contrasting inputs; those results are not available yet.

Rollback returns to the old entry point: if independent dispatch requires simultaneous changes to callers that have not been fully inventoried, or if rollback cannot be done by restoring only the old entry point, stop the trial and do not make the split the default integration approach. Recovery results should be saved alongside the original failure window; later results must not overwrite the earlier assessment.

Still undecided: which caller actually triggers `progress rendering` now; whether it will pass through this split; and how long to retain the old entry point. Until the first two points are clear, this cannot be used to present the completion-stage boundary as an established fact.

# Quality Signal Dashboard: Troubleshooting and Handoff Tree for Blocked Entry Points

When the current entry point is blocked, find the original record first, then decide whether to stay within requirements · Quality Signal Dashboard, exit this round, or hand off to the permissions owner. This tree does not explain the entire call flow; it only prevents a lost incident state from being repackaged as a clean, normal sample.

```text
Is there an original record?
├─ No
│  ├─ Only the final status remains
│  │  └─ Leave it blank; do not write a cause unless the first result can be recovered
│  └─ Even the current entry point cannot be located
│     └─ Exit and wait for entry point information
└─ Yes
   ├─ The requirements-quality-signal identifier is not unique
   │  └─ Distinguish old objects with the same name first; stop further comparison
   ├─ The current results differ between the two environments
   │  └─ Save them separately; do not overwrite one with the other
   ├─ The first result has loaded, but the failure stops after the person on duty
   │  └─ Include the original record and stopping point in the handoff
   └─ The difference is still confined to the Quality Signal Dashboard itself
      └─ Continue within the project
```

## Capture the original state before restoring

The old version treated "green after a rerun" as a starting point for further investigation. Instead, first retain the original input, current entry point, current revision, and first visible result. A rerun is allowed, but it cannot replace that incident state. Without an original record, the tree ends at the first level. In particular, if only the final status remains, do not write in a plausible-looking failure sequence.

The records in CLKB-009 require attaching the requirements-quality-signal from that time, the current entry point, and the first visible current revision back to the incident record. This requirement addresses the missing original state; it does not ask for a second copy of a normal result. If objects with the same name are mixed together, first label their versions clearly according to CLKB-003. Until that is done, there is no basis for comparing subsequent differences.

## When environment results differ

The two environments previously produced different current results, and the command could not be found at the time. Do not collapse the difference into an averaged assessment, or delete one environment's record because the other later recovered. The only action to take is to record each entry point, each first visible result, and what is still missing, separately.

```text
Are both records available?
├─ No
│  └─ Retain only the available record; mark the other as not yet recovered
└─ Yes
   ├─ Is it the same requirements-quality-signal?
   │  ├─ Uncertain: return to the version identifier branch
   │  └─ Yes: compare the first difference side by side
   └─ Has the difference extended beyond the Quality Signal Dashboard itself?
      ├─ No: continue within the project
      └─ Yes: prepare handoff materials
```

CLKB-006 first recorded the inconsistent environment results; the command was still being sought later. So "no command" is not a blank to fill from memory. The record can say that the command was not found, but that does not justify naming a specific command or assigning a cause. If a new read leaves only the final status, treat that as missing the original state too.

## Handoff stopping points

Handoff is not the default action when "the cause cannot be found." Stop this tree when any of the following applies:

- A user-visible interface needs to change, and the existing records cannot establish the ownership boundary;
- The difference extends beyond an identifiable project interface;
- The first visible result is already available, but the subsequent failure stops after the person on duty;
- The records indicate a permissions issue, rather than a resource, index, or same-name object mix-up within the Quality Signal Dashboard itself.

Attach only the original record, version identifier, entry point, current revision, first visible result, and explicit stopping point to the handoff. Do not include guesses about "what it should be." The stopping point in CLKB-009 is "after the person on duty"; this means someone needs to take over here, not that the root cause is known.

If the issue is still confined to the Quality Signal Dashboard, just continue recording it. If the user-visible contract needs to change, this page stops here; open a separate review. CLKB-012 require retaining the old conclusion first, then checking the time difference for the maintenance entry point. Do not silently rewrite an earlier assessment as a new one.

## The remaining blank

The result for the second current revision may still be missing. The approach in CLKB-014 is to recover the second run or read; if only the final status remains, leave it blank. Do not substitute the first record for the second, or use a later green status to fill in an intermediate step.

DOC-34 contain marginal notes on an unresolved incident state. Start there if you need to revisit that state, but the handoff decision still belongs on this page.

# Quality Signal Dashboard Stuck Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

This page still retains an earlier judgment: if it recovers after rerunning, it can initially be treated as an intermittent environment issue. That judgment was not deleted because some people still enter through old links; however, it is no longer suitable as a branching criterion. The problem encountered later was not "can it be run one more time," but that after rerunning, the first failed sample was overwritten, and the results from the two environments were merged into a seemingly smooth record.

Troubleshooting starts from the current entry point. The goal here is narrow: classify the immediate stuck symptom as requirements-quality-signal's own record, a gap requiring exit, or the permissions owner; stop at the first point where there is no new material. It does not reconstruct the process for the caller, nor does it lump same-named objects, environment differences, and subsequent reads into a single cause.

The current maintenance entry is still: `docs/adj-requirements/runbooks/requirements-quality-signal-who to hand off to after getting stuck.md`. This page has been referenced for a long time, but some of its branches are only suitable for the way records were kept at the time. Below, the still-executable sections and the retained old paragraphs are presented together. When taking over, first look at where the symptom occurs; do not just extract a single conclusion.

## What to look at first after entering

"Stuck" does not mean a single kind of failure. The current entry point commonly presents one of the following situations: there is no original record for requirements-quality-signal; the same-named object has no version identifier; the first visible result is still there, but subsequent processing stops after the person on duty; the two environments have different current results; or the second read contains only the final state. Their common point is incomplete information, not a single technical cause.

At the start, retain the following:

- The actual location of the current entry point;
- The name of requirements-quality-signal seen at the time;
- The version identifier that can distinguish an old object with the same name;
- The current revision;
- The first visible result;
- If a second run or read already exists, its relationship to the first one.

"Retain" means attaching existing material back to the incident, not filling in guesses. If any item cannot be found, state explicitly that it was not found. In particular, do not move the later final state back to fill in the first result; the final state only indicates what the page or read showed later and cannot prove what happened initially.

```text
Current entry point
│
├─ Cannot find the original record
│  ├─ Only the final state remains
│  │  └─ Stop: record "First result missing"; do not write the root cause
│  └─ Cannot even determine the entry point location
│     └─ Exit: wait for the entry point or original record
│
└─ Original record found
   ├─ Same-named requirements-quality-signal has not been distinguished by version
   │  └─ Identify the object first; pause comparison
   ├─ Results differ between the two environments
   │  └─ Retain both results side by side; follow the environment branch
   ├─ First result exists; subsequent processing stops after the person on duty
   │  └─ Prepare the handoff with the stopping point
   ├─ Clearly an issue with the Quality Signal Dashboard's own record, resource, or index
   │  └─ Stay within the project
   └─ Already beyond the interface that can be confirmed
      └─ Hand off to the permissions owner; do not continue extending the speculation
```
"Stop" in the tree does not mean abandoning the record. When stopping, leave the last confirmed node and the missing item, so the next person taking over does not have to guess back from the final state to the original situation. Conversely, the tree must not skip over a gap just to obtain a complete answer.

## Original Record Missing

First determine which layer is missing. A missing original record is different from "no problem"; an ambiguously labeled same-name object does not mean that the original record does not exist. If only the page's final state was retained, the record should state that only the final state was seen and that the first visible result could not be recovered. At this point, do not infer what happened in between from later successful reads, directory names, or output from other environments.

CLKB-009 is specifically for leaving this kind of gap: link the requirements-quality-signal from that time, the current entry point, and the first visible current revision back to "who it was handed to after getting stuck"; do not create a new clean sample. Its purpose is to fix the situation at a traceable point, not to require every missing item to be filled in. When there is no first result, avoid all of the following wording:

- "It was probably the same kind of failure";
- "It worked normally after rerunning, so the earlier issue was just intermittent";
- "The final state was normal, so the original record can be ignored";
- "There was no problem in another environment, so there was no problem at the current entry point either".

All of these statements may become clues for later investigation, but they cannot replace the initial record. If all you have at hand is a conjecture, write it as a conjecture and stop here.

Sometimes the entry point is still there, but the attachment or earlier read is gone. Do not mark it as "record complete" just because the entry point exists. The entry point can only help with locating it next time; whether comparison can continue depends on whether the requirements-quality-signal from that time, the version identifier, and the first visible result can be matched. If any one of them is missing, first list the missing item below the incident, then decide whether it is worth continuing to look. If there is no new material, the procedure for leaving this page ends here.

### Old Paragraph: Rerun First, Then Decide

> If rerunning restores it, initially treat it as an environmental intermittent issue; the original record does not need to be pursued.

This section came from the first edition and is retained for people arriving from old links. Subsequent records have shown that it erases the samples that truly need to be compared, so it is no longer used. This correction does not mean rerunning is prohibited; it means that rerunning must come after preserving the original as-is. New results from a rerun should be recorded separately; they must not overwrite the first result or combine the two results into a single continuous phenomenon.

If the original record was already gone before the rerun, the rerun can answer only "whether the same situation can still be seen now", not "why it got stuck at that time". Recording this limitation is more useful than filling in a seemingly complete attribution.

## Same-Name Objects and Version Identifiers

When requirements-quality-signal has the same name but is missing a version identifier, do not compare the results directly. First separate the old same-name objects. CLKB-003 points exactly to this issue: the referenced requirements-quality-signal must have its version clearly labeled, and old same-name objects must not be mixed together.

Separating them does not require adding naming rules or guessing inheritance relationships between objects. Simply keep the existing names, version identifiers, current revision and entry points separate for each observed instance. Leave the one without a version identifier unconfirmed, rather than filling it in based on the newer object. The following branch applies to this type of situation:

```text
Same name; can the versions distinguish them?
├─ Yes
│  ├─ The current entry point and the first result belong to the same object
│  │  └─ Comparison can continue
│  └─ The entry point or result belongs to another object
│     └─ Record them separately; do not merge them into a single stuck incident
└─ No
   ├─ The version identifier can be recovered
   │  └─ Recover it, then follow the comparison branch
   └─ It cannot be recovered
      └─ Stop: mark "same-name objects not separated"
```

The stop condition for this step is clear: if you cannot confirm which same-name object the entry point and the first result belong to, do not pass the "difference" to the next level. One object working normally and another being stuck cannot serve as evidence that "the same Quality Signal Console gets stuck intermittently". Conversely, even if both objects show similar behavior, do not treat them as one event just because they have the same name.

In old records, version identifiers were sometimes added to the final notes, making it read as though the comparison had already been completed. That style makes it easy to see the conclusion first and only later discover that the objects are not the same. Object identification should now come before the branch. Old records do not need to be cleaned up, but do not follow their ordering when taking over.

## Different results in two environments

The situation recorded in CLKB-006 was: the current results in the two environments differed, and the command had not been found at the time; efforts to add the command afterward were still ongoing, and the record retained only the differing current results. The easiest mistakes here are to expand "different environments" into a known cause, or to treat the side that recovered later as a stand-in for the other side.

The environment branch does only three things: save each side separately, confirm whether they refer to the same object, and find the first point of divergence. Do not compress the two sides into an averaged description, and do not fill gaps on one side with the final state of the other.

```text
Are records available from both environments?
├─ No
│  ├─ Only one environment's current result was found
│  │  └─ Keep that result; write "not recovered" for the other environment
│  └─ Only final states remain for both environments
│     └─ Stop: the first difference cannot be compared
└─ Yes
   ├─ Object versions have not been separated
   │  └─ Return to the same-name object branch
   ├─ Both first visible results are available
   │  └─ Find the first difference side by side
   └─ One side's first result is missing
      └─ Record only the asymmetry; do not make a judgment about the cause
```

"The command had not been found at the time" should retain its original meaning: no command was available to attach at that time. This does not mean that no such command exists, much less that one can be written from memory. If a new way to read the data is found later, it applies only to subsequent records; it must not make the earlier situation look as though the same material was already available then.

When recording the results side by side, a minimal table can be used:

| Item | Environment One | Environment Two |
| --- | --- | --- |
| requirements-quality-signal | Existing name or missing | Existing name or missing |
| Version identifier | Confirmed or unconfirmed | Confirmed or unconfirmed |
| Current entry point | Known location or not recovered | Known location or not recovered |
| First visible result | Original text retained or missing | Original text retained or missing |
| Subsequent reads | Present, absent, or only the final state remains | Present, absent, or only the final state remains |

"Missing" in the table is itself a result and should not be cleaned up into a blank. The first difference between the two sides may simply mean that the objects have not been distinguished, or that one entry point is later than the other; further discussion of environment differences is only necessary when the objects and time points can already be aligned. If they cannot be aligned, stop at the table and do not turn it into a root-cause narrative.

### An earlier incorrect merge

An old record described the results from two locations as "the current results are unstable". This description was too broad, making it impossible later to tell which location, which object, or which read appeared first. That section is still in an old attachment and should not be used as a new handoff summary. At a minimum, the new summary should state separately whether the result exists at each location; if it is missing on one side, state that it is missing rather than describing it as "intermittent".

## The first result has loaded, but subsequent progress stops after the person on duty

After CLKB-009, a more specific situation appeared: the current result had loaded, but the failure stopped after the person on duty. This wording only marks the last visible stopping point; it does not provide a root cause or say who should fix it. Therefore, "after the person on duty" must not be rewritten as a specific module, caller, or permission check.

The handling sequence is as follows:

1. Confirm that "loaded" refers to the current result, not the final state from a later rerun.
2. Put the current revision, the first visible result, and the last stopping point in the same section of the record.
3. Check whether the issue before the stopping point still concerns the Quality Signal Dashboard's own records, resources, or indexes.
4. If it has already passed the interface that can be confirmed, stop breaking it down further and prepare for handoff.
5. If unresolved same-named objects or environment differences remain before the stopping point, go back and address those earlier branches first.

There is no requirement here to reconstruct the person on duty's handling process as a timeline. What can be confirmed is that "the failure stopped after the person on duty"; what cannot be confirmed is what happened afterward. The handoff materials should preserve this distinction. Describing the unknown part as "waiting for confirmation from the other party" is acceptable; describing it as "a root cause that the other party is responsible for" is not.

Some records may look nearly complete because the current result has already loaded. Do not skip verification against the original on that basis. Successful loading only means that one node is visible, not that the subsequent assessment is already established. If the current result corresponds to another object with the same name, or if that result comes from another environment, return to the earlier branch.

## Cases that stay within the project

This page keeps only the following within requirements · Quality Signal Dashboard for further work: the original records, identifiers for objects with the same name, the Quality Signal Dashboard's own resources or indexes, and read information that can still be filled in through existing entry points. Here, "keeping it within the project" does not mean external influences have already been ruled out; it means the available materials have not yet crossed an interface that can be confirmed.

When keeping it within the project, the record should continue to focus on the missing item, rather than starting a separate, generic investigation. For example:

- If the original record is gone, continue looking for the first visible result, without discussing environmental causes at the same time;
- If objects with the same name have not been distinguished, first add version identifiers, rather than comparing the two for differences;
- If the two environments are inconsistent, retain the results side by side, rather than treating a green status on one side as recovery on the other;
- If the second read is missing, mark the second read of the current revision as not yet filled in, rather than substituting the final state.

This may make the record look as though it is not reaching closure quickly, but it avoids lumping multiple unconfirmed points together and pushing them onto the permissions owner. Leave this page only when the issue clearly crosses an interface, requires a change to the user-visible contract, or the existing stopping point is no longer within the scope that the Quality Signal Dashboard can confirm.

CLKB-012 is a reminder that there is a timing gap for the maintenance entry point, and that the old conclusion should be retained for now. This reminder also applies to branches that continue within the project: do not rewrite an old record to say "the entry point was clear at the time" just because an entry point can be found today. An old conclusion can be marked as no longer applicable later, but should not be silently replaced.

## Stopping points before handoff to the permissions owner

Handoff is not the default exit for "cannot find the cause". Prepare a handoff only when enough diagnostic material is already available from the situation and the issue is beyond what this page can confirm. Any of the following can serve as a stopping point:

- The user-visible contract needs to change;
- A difference has been confirmed to cross a project interface;
- The first visible result is already available, and subsequent steps clearly stop after the person on duty;
- The available materials point directly to a permissions issue, rather than missing original records, object identifiers, resources, or indexes;
- The timing gap between the current entry point and the maintenance entry point means the old assessment can no longer be applied.

The handoff package does not need to be a complete incident review. Simply attach the available original records, object version identifiers, current entry point, current revision, first visible result, whether the second read exists, whether the environments are inconsistent, and the last confirmed stopping point. If any item is missing, state that it is missing. Do not add commands, module names, or call relationships just to make the package look complete.

```text
Prepare handoff
├─ Can describe the last confirmed stopping point
│  ├─ Original record is still available
│  │  └─ Attach the original record and version, entry point, and first result
│  └─ Items are missing from the original record
│     └─ Attach the available parts, and specify which item is missing
└─ Cannot describe the stopping point
   ├─ It is merely "stuck"
   │  └─ Return to the current entry point, fill in the record or exit
   └─ Only the final state remains
      └─ Do not hand off for root-cause investigation; record the missing information as-is
```

What the permissions owner receives is a situation with clear boundaries, not a conclusion that the current page has reached on their behalf. If, after handoff, the issue turns out to still involve objects with the same name, an entry-point timing gap, or a missing second read, return it to the corresponding branch and retain a trace of the fact that this handoff occurred, rather than rewriting it as though it was never handed off.

## No result from the second read of the current revision

CLKB-014 The gap left by this is specific: restore the current revision from the second run or read; if only the final state remains, leave it blank. This branch cannot be closed with "there is already a record from the first time," because the materials from the two runs serve different purposes.

When the second result exists, first place it after the first result as the second result; do not merge it into the initial description. It can show what was read later, but it cannot automatically prove that the first failure has disappeared. When the second result is missing, there is also no need to invalidate the first result; simply state that the two cannot be compared.

```text
Can the second run or read be found?
├─ Yes
│  ├─ The current revision is identifiable
│  │  └─ List it alongside the first; do not replace the first
│  └─ The revision is still unclear
│     └─ Retain the read and mark the version as unconfirmed
└─ No
   ├─ Only the final state remains
   │  └─ Leave the second result blank; do not backfill
   └─ There is no subsequent material at all
      └─ End this branch
```

Someone previously interpreted a missing second result as "there is no need to look again." That does not apply here. The absence itself affects environment comparisons and handoff materials: if the two environments each have only a final state from a different time, you cannot claim that they behaved differently under the same conditions; if the first result is clear and the second is missing, you can only state that the subsequent read did not recover it.

## Chronologically preserved notes

The following are not new operating steps, but several old records that affect the reading order. They are retained to explain why this page now puts "as-is" and "stopping point" first.

- CLKB-006 An environment result mismatch appeared first, and it was subsequently classified as needing further handling. Later records still said the command was being filled in, indicating that at the time only different current results could be compared.
- CLKB-003 It was handled later, with the focus on clearly labeling the version of the same-named requirements-quality-signal, rather than creating a new result to replace the old object.
- CLKB-009 After the risk check and handoff, it left the boundary "current result loaded; failure stopped with the person on duty." This is much narrower than "loaded, therefore complete."
- CLKB-003 It was blocked again because the failure sample provided by the caller was missing. This blockage does not mean that other samples can be used as substitutes; it specifically shows why the missing sample should remain missing.
- CLKB-012 It requires checking the time and context of the maintenance entry, while retaining the old conclusion for now. It does not authorize using a new entry to rewrite the old context.
- CLKB-014 It still requires a second current revision to be added; if only the final state remains, continue leaving it blank.

These additions do not form a complete causal chain. They separately explain why the object, environment, stopping point, and second read cannot be merged into one statement that "the quality signal desk is unstable." When entering from an old link, first compare which item the context you have belongs to, then use the tree above.

## Old entry and time gap

The maintenance entry may be later than the live context, or it may retain earlier wording. When there is such a time gap, first distinguish two things: whether the entry can still be located, and whether the judgment in the entry belongs to the context at that time. The former can help find the materials; the latter must be determined by the object version, current revision, and first visible result.

Do not conclude that the old context is equally complete just because the entry file exists now; and do not skip preserving the environment results side by side just because the old entry says "the environment is intermittent." CLKB-012's "retain the old conclusion for now" means here that the old text remains readable, but the new investigation does not route directly based on the old conclusion.

If the current entry has the same name as the old record, still first check whether the requirements-quality-signal it points to is the same. The same name, the same entry, and the same final state are all insufficient substitutes for a version identifier. When it cannot be determined, writing "entry visible, object unconfirmed" in the record is more accurate than forcing a continuation.

## Minimal record format when taking over

Below is one format that can be left directly beside the live context. It is not a form that must be filled out completely; leave any unavailable content as "not recovered."

```text
Current entry:
requirements-quality-signal:
Version identifier:
Current revision:
First visible result:
Second run or read: yes / no / only the final state remains
Environment: one / two different / not compared
Last confirmed stopping point:
Reason for keeping it in the project or handing it off:
```

Under "Reason for keeping it in the project or handing it off," write only the boundary, for example, "Same-named objects could not be distinguished; stop comparing," "The current result is loaded; subsequent work stops after the person on duty," or "The user-visible contract needs to change." Do not write "It is probably a problem somewhere." If the reason is still "cannot tell," return to the original-record branch at the top, or exit and wait for more material.

This format also prevents another old mistake: recording everything next to the final processing result. The original record, the first result, and the second read should retain their chronological relationship; a later green status must not swallow the missing field above it.

## Boundary with related records

CLKB-003, CLKB-006, CLKB-009, CLKB-012 and CLKB-014 are the related cards that this page can navigate to. They help locate the object identifier, environmental differences, the original state, the time discrepancy at the maintenance entry point, and the gap in the second current revision, respectively. When you need to review unresolved on-site margin notes, DOC-34 can serve as an adjacent record; do not infer unwritten commands, call relationships, or specific fixes from these cards.

The end conditions for this page are explicit: either the situation is still within the range that can be confirmed by the quality signal desk, and the gap should remain documented; or the interface has been crossed, and the last confirmed stopping point is handed off to the permission owner; or the original record is insufficient, in which case exit without assigning a cause. The old practice of "treating it as intermittent once it recovers after a rerun" remains documented, but no longer overrides these stopping conditions.

# Quality Signal Desk Responsibility Boundaries

When the temporary maintainer receives a failing sample, first check whether it is already within the project's intake scope for handling. The only items that can be taken over directly at present are due items under "exit actions." This scope covers due-date checks, handling records for due items, and leaving the handling result at the original intake point; it does not cover explaining the behavior of `requirements-quality-signal`, or deciding on the original owner's behalf which layer a test failure sample belongs to.

| Observed item | Primary contact | Scope they can handle | Outside the temporary handoff scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Due items under exit actions | Temporary maintainer | Verify due items, perform or record the exit action | Redefine the exit criteria |
| Behavior explanation for `requirements-quality-signal` | Original owner | Explain existing behavior and applicable scope | Temporary maintainer answering on their behalf |
| Failure samples generated around test | Original owner | Determine whether the sample should be included in regression stratification | Assigning an owner based only on the most recent reply |
| Attribution of unstable signals | Original owner | Retain the sample and state the required context | Temporary maintainer consolidating it into a conclusion |
| Long-term handoff owner for `prompt lifecycle` | Unconfirmed | Project intake holds the issue and placeholder | Writing the most recent respondent in as the owner |
| Project intake | requirements · Quality Signal Desk on-duty person | Hand off after receiving the object, time, and minimum observed symptom | Providing a unified explanation for the three technical scopes |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[Failing sample or unstable signal] --> Q{Is it a due item under exit actions}
    Q -- Yes --> M[Temporary maintainer]
    M --> X[Handle the due item and leave a record]
    Q -- No --> O[requirements-quality-signal original owner]
    O --> R[Behavior explanation, regression stratification, or signal attribution]
    Q -- Cannot determine --> P[Project intake retains the placeholder and hands off]
```

The handoff includes only three things: the object name, the time it was first seen, and the minimum observed symptom. If the issue concerns `requirements-quality-signal`'s behavior, the temporary maintainer hands the intake back to the original owner; they must not continue handling the subsequent technical judgments just because they completed the due action. If the original owner cannot be found temporarily, the placeholder remains visible; the on-duty person may coordinate a contact window, but does not treat that coordination as long-term ownership.

Record status changes in Board, put confirmed long-term guidance in Docs, and leave failure output and unstable signals observed in the field in the project conversation first. When reviewing across surfaces, navigate only from the project intake; do not write separate copies of the explanation in multiple places. Related navigation cards: `CLKB-002`, `CLKB-005`, `CLKB-013`. The long-term maintenance entry remains `docs/adj-requirements/ownership/adj-requirements-Temporary Handoff Boundaries.md`; the body and attachments are maintained by the adj-requirements project.
