# On-call procedure for a failed documentation site run

This page is still organized around the incident state from one failed artwork-documentation-portal run. It is not a general pre-release checklist: the on-call engineer must preserve the first visible difference, follow the documentation site entry point used at the time to the first stop point, and leave recovery actions that have not been performed for later assessment. The entry points, terminology, and sequence on this page retain their original time context; if the incident state differs from the page as it stands, do not start by rewriting the old record as a new conclusion.

## After receiving a report of an abnormal run

First, copy down the state as it is, before tidying anything up. Preserve the original input, the version used at the time, and the first visible result; if a known-good sample is already available, use it only to find the first difference. Do not restart to get more information, refresh permissions, or recreate data. Those actions change the incident state, making it impossible to tell later whether the difference appeared in the original run or was introduced by the response actions.

The entry point is still `docs/adj-artwork/runbooks/artwork-User documentation site-On-call page for one failed run.md`. First confirm that you are looking at this user documentation site run, rather than treating another docs page or another project's page as the same object. The documentation site discussed here covers the user entry points built around docs, version notes, and handling of outdated content; it has its own schedule, maintainers, and exit conditions. If you cannot identify the object at the outset, record only the entry point and what you see, and do not continue applying the steps below.

The old version named the first checkpoint `progress rendering`. That term remains here because handoff records and early incident records used it to locate the checkpoint. Once there, first check whether `filesystem fixtures` has already appeared:

- If it has, do not clean up fixtures or prepare the directory again to make it look normal. Record whether it was already present before entry or appeared only after reaching this point.
- If it has not, do not record "not seen" as success either. Preserve the steps already taken and the results displayed at the time, then return to the most recent known-good sample to check whether the first difference occurred before this point.
- Change only one condition when comparing. Do not replace the input, version, entry point, and preserved incident state all at once, or subsequent comparisons will be meaningless.

This procedure is meant to pin down the failure boundary, not to cover every combination in one exercise. Early pages treated `filesystem fixtures` as a strong clue; in an incident, it only shows that the on-call engineer reached a state that can be preserved. It does not replace subsequent confirmation of the source.

## Stop point

Next, look for `parameter provenance`. If it does not appear, stop. The stop point does not mean waiting for someone to fill in the blank with a default value. It means stating clearly at handoff which section of the documentation site page the run reached, what the last visible state was, which known-good sample was compared earlier, and which actions were deliberately not performed.

One old limitation remains here: the recovery actions have not been tried in the shared environment. The on-call engineer therefore should not write "the service opens again" as completed recovery, much less perform unverified return actions just to get a green status quickly. The original incident state takes priority over the tidied-up state; even if the latter looks normal, it cannot overwrite the record of the former.

If the first difference extends beyond the documentation site's own scope—for example, it no longer concerns only docs user entry points, version notes, or handling of outdated content, but involves a shared interface—the documentation site side hands over only the entry point and the observed behavior, leaving further assessment to the shared interface's maintainer. The documentation site still retains user communication and the run record on this page. Do not describe a local recovery as recovery of all related objects.

## Handoff note

At handoff, write beside the corresponding step on this page; there is no need to create a separate summary. Leave at least four things:

1. The actions actually performed, and whether the run stopped before or after the action;
2. Hypotheses that were ruled out. Keep hypotheses that have not been checked marked as unconfirmed;
3. The maintainer that `parameter provenance` pointed to at the time, or "not yet found";
4. The entry point where the next check should begin, rather than working backward from the tidied-up result.

When someone other than the author reproduces the run, stop if any prerequisite state is missing; do not fill it in from memory. Records that need comparison with the current revision go separately in DOC-37; this page retains only the entry, first difference, and stop location for this failed run.

## Retained old notes

The earliest version said only, "Find `progress rendering`; if you see `filesystem fixtures`, do not clean up the incident state; stop if `parameter provenance` is missing." This sequence has not been deleted because it can still help the next on-call engineer get back to the first failure at the time. The original input, version, first result, and known-good sample were added later to prevent on-call engineers from doing recovery first and then guessing where the failure began.

The page once called a later location `completion dispatch`, while some other handoff records used `help formatting`. These should serve only as location terms in old records, not as grounds to expand the scope of the run on this page. If the incident only reached the earlier stop point, record that honestly and stop there; without new incident evidence, do not interpret these terms as confirmed causes.

This page can still be used to review old runs, but the recovery section has limited applicability as executable steps. Whoever takes over should first preserve the state they see, then continue from the entry points and stop points recorded here.

# Compatibility Directory Window Closeout Checklist

At window closeout, handle only the borrowed items, final output, return deadlines, and revocation entry point left by the active entry point. Migration records and caller compatibility in the compatibility directory are still maintained in their respective materials; this checklist tells whoever closes the window when they can stop and when they must preserve the state.

First open `docs/adj-parameter-contract/release/Parameter-contract-compatibility-directory-short-checklist-before-window-close.md`. It is the handoff entry point for this round of the checklist; there is no need to copy the attachment contents onto this page. Before starting, record the active entry point, original input, observed version, and first visible result. If any of these were recovered only after temporary diagnostics, mark them separately; do not combine them with the original state in one record.

## Closeout Actions

1. **Mark where the entry point changed.**
   - [ ] If the active entry point has changed, put the time of the change beside the record.
   - [ ] Review the statistics before and after the change separately; do not subtract them directly. This is the reminder left by CLKD-003: once a trend crosses an entry-point change, it is no longer the same sample segment.
   - [ ] If the earliest result can no longer be found, stop comparing. Do not use green results compiled later to fill in the starting point.

2. **Preserve the gaps.**
   - [ ] Compare parameter-contract-compatibility-catalog with the active entry point.
   - [ ] Leave intervening windows with no records blank; do not infer that they passed from adjacent results.
   - [ ] If a rerun is needed, keep its input and first result separately; rerun results establish only what happened in that rerun.

   Completion of CLKD-007 did not fill the earlier gaps in the records, so this step is not a formatting check. The blanks are still information that must be handed over at window closeout.

3. **Check both sample types.**
   - [ ] Keep a sample of the project's success path.
   - [ ] Keep a sample of one rejection path as well.
   - [ ] Samples must correspond to the active entry point. Do not substitute an isolated "success" in the logs for the final output.

   `completion dispatch` can be used as a search term to locate this output, but finding the term is not a reason to skip the output itself. If the output and original input are not in the same place, put the borrowed items on hold first. Do not create a matching record just to finish the closeout.

4. **Reclaim temporary items.**
   - [ ] State the latest return deadline for each borrowed item.
   - [ ] Remove temporary permissions and bypasses before closing the window, then confirm that no new work is still being admitted.
   - [ ] Keep the final output after the return is complete; do not delete the output first and then ask whether the borrowed items have been reclaimed.

   An unclear return status, an inaccessible revocation entry point, or a bypass still in use all mean the window is not closed. In that case, restore the entry point to its state before borrowing, preserve the recorded inputs and outputs, and keep the window marked as unfinished.

5. **Record only the actual handoff destination.**
   - [ ] Put unfinished items beside the specific recipient and entry point.
   - [ ] Remove groups that have been taken offline from the new entry point.
   - [ ] Check the handoff record against the action routing in Parameter contract · Compatibility Directory.

   CLKD-010 is used to find the actual handoff destination; it cannot replace revocation or establish that missing windows have been handled.

## When to Stop

If any of the following occurs, do not compress the records further or mark the window complete:

- The active entry point, original input, or first visible result is missing;
- Before-and-after samples cross an entry-point change but have not been split into segments;
- A borrowed item has no return deadline, or new work is still entering after revocation;
- Diagnostics have changed the state, so the original records and subsequent results cannot be compared directly.

After stopping, first preserve the original input, final output, and blank intervals. Revocation applies only to this round's temporary permissions or bypasses; if it would cross the active interface boundary, leave it at the entry point for handoff rather than expanding the scope of this checklist.

## Handling Older Entries

Version 1 used the appearance of `filesystem fixtures` as the sole stopping criterion. That wording is retained for the state at the time, but no longer determines window closeout on its own. Check entry-point changes, record gaps, returns of borrowed items, and the revocation entry point first. The fixture can still serve as a clue, but does not replace these four checks.

# Dependency boundary troubleshooting and handoff tree

This old workflow still starts with the symptoms visible at the current entry point, but a green rerun no longer means the original failure has cleared. When troubleshooting, first retain the original input, source revision, and first visible result; the second run can only serve as an additional sample. Start at `docs/adj-parameter-help/runbooks/parameter-help-supply-boundary-Who to hand off to when stuck.md`.

## Choose a branch first

```text
Can you get the original records?
├─ No
│  └─ Go back to the earliest dependency source that can be reconstructed; if none is available, record only the gap
└─ Yes
   ├─ Can you follow the source revision to find the original records for the current revision?
   │  ├─ Yes: compare the first point of difference
   │  └─ No: record where the trace breaks; don't guess from directory names or display text
   └─ Has the exit entry point actually been run on the user side?
      ├─ No: stop at the exit entry point
      └─ Yes: check whether the old relationship remains after withdrawal
```

An early version put `prompt lifecycle`, `callback forwarding`, and `completion dispatch` in a fixed order. That was a note left from one lookup at the time; it should no longer be used to rule out issues with dependency sources, licenses, or adoption scope. These terms are now only pointers within old samples: not seeing them does not mean the issue has been assigned to a particular owner.

## Missing original records

When original records are missing, first check whether the dependency source can be traced back along revisions to the earliest reconstructable point. CLKE-002 preserve that source trace; if only the final display is visible, do not use its content to fill in intermediate relationships. CLKE-009 record cases where no reconstructable source was available: if evidence still cannot be found, hide the explanation rather than fill in a seemingly complete conclusion.

The stop condition here is simple: stop as soon as the next step would require guessing the source, guessing the adopter, or substituting an average result for the first failure. Leave the source revision already found, the missing segment, and the symptoms at the entry point together for the person taking over.

## Input fields not confirmed

If the interface side has not yet confirmed the input fields, do not attribute the symptoms to Parameter help · Dependency Boundary Audit itself. CLKE-005 were later blocked because the upstream interface owner had not yet confirmed the input fields; in this situation, the workflow is only responsible for saving the sample from the current entry point and handing the unconfirmed fields back to the interface side. The temporary assignee handles only actions that are due, not the project's long-term implications.

Only continue checking dependency sources and adoption scope if the fields have been confirmed and the discrepancy still lies within this project. Do not change two conditions at once for a comparison; otherwise, it will be impossible to say later which one changed the result.

## Exit actions

After one classification in CLKE-008, a note was added: the one just shown came from the internal view; the user side of the exit entry point had not been run. The internal view and the user-side entry point therefore cannot substitute for each other. If the user side has not yet been run, leave the issue at the exit entry point; do not close it based on internal records.

When an old relationship needs to be withdrawn, replay the exit actions corresponding to CLKE-006, then check whether the old edge has disappeared. That card was later completed as part of a maintenance batch, but the completion record does not establish that every entry point was verified; this workflow still requires retaining the original records from both before and after withdrawal.

## What to write in the handoff

The handoff needs only four items: the symptoms seen at the current entry point, whether original records exist, the source revision that can be located, and the node where the tree stopped. If it stopped at field confirmation, hand it to the interface owner; if it stopped at the user-side exit entry point, hand it to the person responsible for that entry point; if it stopped because the source could not be reconstructed, return to the tracing work in CLKE-002 and CLKE-009.

The old instruction, "continue when you see completion dispatch," is retained above for reference when reading old records. It is no longer a closure condition.

# Troubleshooting tree for handing off blocked dependency-boundary issues

When the explanation at the entry point is blocked, the dependency source is unclear, or an exit action appears not to have taken effect, first preserve the input and result you saw the first time. This process works down from the current entry point for Parameter help · Dependency Boundary Audit; it retains old judgments from several maintenance rounds, so it is suitable for reviewing archived cases. Not every sentence should be treated as a current interface definition.

The path is still `docs/adj-parameter-help/runbooks/parameter-help-supply-boundary-Who to hand off to when blocked.md`. After opening it, you do not need to investigate every branch at once. First answer this: is what you have an original record? If not, the only next step is to find the source, not to fill in intermediate relationships from the user-facing display.

## What to preserve before starting

At a minimum, preserve the behavior observed at the current entry point, the original input, the first visible result, and any source revision you can obtain. Here, "first" means the run before any rerun for troubleshooting; a later retry that turns green shows, at most, that the new run did not exhibit the same behavior again. It cannot replace the old sample.

In one earlier case, retrying too soon left only processed results in the record. After that, the original process added a reminder to "preserve the sample first," but did not fill in all recovery actions. Recovery steps for the shared environment have also never been confirmed in this record. If recovery is needed, do not execute the old paragraphs directly.

If the original record already includes environment differences, preserve those as well. Environment differences only explain why two samples cannot be compared directly; they are not root-cause labels. In particular, do not overwrite the first failure with directory names, averages, or the final display.

## Search order for the old entry point

The original tree contained only three terms: `prompt lifecycle`, `callback forwarding`, and `completion dispatch`. The instructions at the time were to find the first term in the path, then continue through the other two; stop if `completion dispatch` could not be found.

This section is still retained because some old cases were recorded in this order:

```text
Is prompt lifecycle visible?
├─ No: The entry-point record is incomplete; stay at the entry point for now
└─ Yes: Continue looking for callback forwarding
   ├─ Present: The old notes require checking completion dispatch next
   └─ Absent: Preserve the first failing sample and wait for more clues
```

It was later found that this was not a reliable classification tree. The three terms only show how the old samples were searched. They neither prove that the dependency source has been established nor automatically assign the issue to a particular permissions owner. When using this page now, you can use them to locate old records, but do not treat "seeing" or "not seeing" one of these terms as a reason to stop.

## First ask where the original record is

```text
Is there an original record?
├─ No
│  ├─ Can you trace back from the source revision to the earliest reconstructable source?
│  │  ├─ Yes: Record the source location, then compare the current entry point
│  │  └─ No: Log the gap and stop
│  └─ Do not infer backward from display text, directory names, or processed results
└─ Yes
   ├─ Can it be linked to the original record for the current revision?
   │  ├─ Yes: Find only the first difference
   │  └─ No: Write down the break point and hand off to source tracing
   └─ Then enter the exit-entry-point or field-confirmation branch
```

The direction for CLKE-002 is to follow the revision of parameter-help-supply-boundary back to the earliest reconstructable source. The key here is not to write out a very long chain, but to let the next person know which is the earliest available record and where the chain breaks after that. When only the final display is available, the record should explicitly state "the display cannot provide intermediate relationships," rather than filling the explanation page with guesses.

CLKE-009 corresponds to another situation: adj-parameter-help lacks a reconstructable source. The action recorded on that card was to look for evidence; when there is no evidence, hide the explanation rather than add a conclusion. This may seem conservative, but it is better than allowing an unsourced judgment about dependencies to keep being cited. The branch for a missing original record ends here; it should not also move into a discussion of exit actions or adoption scope.

If you can trace from the source revision to the original record for the current revision, write down the first location where the two sides differ. Do not list every difference at once, and do not retroactively insert later differences into the earliest sample. This process is looking for a break point that determines where the next step belongs, not reconstructing the entire history of the project.

## User-facing exit entry point

Internal views can easily mislead the assessment of exit actions. After a failed classification, CLKE-008 added a case note: what had just been checked was the internal view, and the user-facing side of the exit entry point had not been run. Therefore, the internal view can serve as a record that has been reviewed, but it cannot prove that the user-facing entry point has followed the same path.

First distinguish between two states here:

```text
Has the user-facing side of the exit entry point been run?
├─ Not run
│  └─ Stop at the user-facing entry point; do not close the issue using the internal view
└─ Run
   ├─ Original record available: Check whether the old relationship still exists before and after exit
   └─ No original record: Return to the source branch; do not draw a conclusion about the exit result
```

When an old relationship needs to be withdrawn, replay the exit action corresponding to CLKE-006 and verify that the old edge has actually disappeared. The "old edge" is the relationship that previously still linked the dependency source to the adoption scope; do not assume that the relationship has been withdrawn just because it is no longer visible on the page. Save the records from before and after withdrawal separately so that the later result does not overwrite the earlier behavior.

CLKE-006 was later completed as a small change in a maintenance batch. This completion status indicates that the actions listed on that card have been handled, not that every entry point, historical record, or explanation has been reverified. If the user-facing side has not been run, still stop at the first branch above.

## When input fields have not been confirmed

CLKE-005 was once blocked because the upstream interface owner had not yet confirmed the input fields. In this scenario, the entry-point side should not assume what the fields mean just to advance the investigation, nor should it turn unconfirmed fields into long-term rules for Parameter help · Dependency Boundary Audit.

Handle this in the following order:

```text
Have the field meanings been confirmed?
├─ No: Preserve the current sample and field names, and hand off to the interface side
└─ Yes
   ├─ The difference is still in this project's sources or explanations: Continue checking adoption scope
   └─ The difference crosses a known interface: Hand off with the break point; do not keep guessing
```

When fields are unconfirmed, the temporary assignee should only perform the actions for the current round: save the sample, mark the unconfirmed fields, and explain which level of the tree has been reached. Do not broaden the meaning of license, dependency source, or exit responsibility on behalf of the interface side. Only after the fields have been confirmed, and if the difference remains within the project, is there a reason to continue examining adoption scope; if the difference has already crossed a defined interface, the current record should stop there.

Change only one condition at a time when comparing. This restriction comes from lessons learned in old cases: after changing the entry point, record, or fields at the same time, even if the result changes, it is impossible to attribute the change to any one item. A single-condition comparison does not guarantee finding the root cause, but at least it does not mix new uncertainty into the existing break point.

## Adoption scope and exit responsibility

Discuss adoption scope only after the source can be reconstructed and the fields have been confirmed. There is no need to write a general dependency policy here; just determine whether the current behavior is within Parameter help · Dependency Boundary Audit's own explanations, resources, or indexes, or has crossed into an external interface.

For cases within the project, continue preserving the entry-point record and the first difference, and handle them according to the project's maintenance cadence. For cases that cross an interface, the handoff materials should include the location of the original record, the source revision, the confirmed input fields, and the stopping node. Without these, the next assignee can only collect data again from the entry point, not start from a one-line conclusion.

Do not mix exit responsibility with adoption scope. Adoption scope answers which side is using this relationship; exit responsibility answers who needs to verify that the old edge has disappeared. When the former is still unclear, do not pretend that the latter has been completed; when the latter requires user-facing verification, do not substitute an internal view.

## Handoff package

This long process actually requires handing off only the following targeted materials:

| Situation | What to preserve | Handoff destination |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original record cannot be found | Current entry-point behavior, source revision checked, break point | Source tracing for CLKE-002 or CLKE-009 |
| Fields unconfirmed | Original input, unconfirmed fields, first result | Upstream interface owner |
| User-facing exit not run | Document the internal view separately from the fact that the user-facing side was not run | Exit-entry-point side |
| Old edge remains after withdrawal | Records from before and after withdrawal, location of the old edge | Maintenance action corresponding to CLKE-006 |
| Difference remains within the project | First difference, adoption scope | Internal maintenance for Parameter help · Dependency Boundary Audit |

The "handoff destination" in the table does not mean that all issues should be opened for the same kind of handling. When the source is missing, the primary gap is reconstructable evidence; when fields are unconfirmed, the primary gap is an interface explanation; when the user-facing side has not been run, the primary gap is an entry-point result. None of these three can substitute for another.

The subsequent statuses of CLKE-005, CLKE-006, and CLKE-008 should not be pieced together into a single conclusion either: one was once blocked pending field confirmation, one records a completed small change, and another revealed that the user-facing exit entry point had not been run. They are included in this process so that investigators can find the historical entry points at the corresponding nodes, not to prove that the same cause covers every situation.

## Old judgments still retained

The old draft said, "Continue after seeing `completion dispatch`; stop if it is not seen." In the early stages, this could prevent jumping to a final cause without evidence, but it mistook a search term for a boundary. It should now be changed to: if there is no original record, stop at the source; if the user-facing side has not been run, stop at the exit entry point; if fields are unconfirmed, stop at the interface explanation. The old sentence is retained only to explain why the investigation did not continue at the time when reading old case records.

The old draft also described a green rerun result as something too close to successful recovery. That wording was later dropped. A green result can be saved with the sample, but it cannot overwrite the first failure or cancel the original exit verification or source tracing.

The TODO for shared-environment recovery actions has not been completed and remains near the old version. When recovery is needed, obtain the operational records available at that time separately; do not interpret gaps in this process as steps that are authorized for execution.

## Stopping points

Stop when you reach a point that requires new evidence: do not continue if you need to guess the dependency source, guess field meanings, treat an internal view as a user-facing result, or infer an old relationship backward from the page display. Stopping does not mean closing the issue; it tells the next assignee exactly which kind of record is currently missing.

Related issues can be recorded separately. Do not make the current path take over all explanations, all adopters, and all exit actions at once. If you only want to verify whether the old edge has disappeared, take the exit branch with the records from before and after withdrawal; if you only want to find the earliest source, follow the revision along the source branch. Both paths stop when original records are insufficient, but they stop for different reasons.

Finally, review once more: if the conclusion in hand is supported only by display text, strip it back to "not yet reconstructed"; if it is supported only by an internal view, strip it back to "user-facing side not run"; if fields are still unconfirmed, strip it back to the field break point. The resulting record may not look polished, but it preserves what was actually observed at the time.

# Version Freeze Window Deviation Postmortem

During the version freeze window, the actual visible result did not match the original plan. When this was first noticed, the team on site provisionally recorded it as calls during the window not being applied as planned; this was only a working judgment to facilitate continued investigation and cannot yet be treated as the cause.

At the time, few things could be confirmed: the deviation was discovered during the window; the minimal call log retained the result seen at discovery; and, to keep things moving, the team used a reversible old entry point for temporary recovery. The recovery action cleared the immediate blockage but did not explain where the result changed.

The impact scope was not quantified. The logs show a discrepancy between the plan and the result, but cannot establish whether the same phenomenon had already occurred outside the window or list the callers actually affected. Whether the old entry point covered all paths, and whether recovery changed the observation conditions, also remain unanswered.

The investigation reviewed the call names and `src/click/utils.py`. This location was only a lookup point encountered at the time, not confirmed ownership. The cause, the long-term entry point, and who will coordinate subsequent records have not been settled.

# Postmortem of the Deviation During the Version Freeze Window

During the version freeze window, the original plan and the visible results diverged. As the window proceeded according to the original plan, the results observed on the ground did not follow that plan; this was initially recorded as "calls during the freeze did not take effect as expected." This assessment was useful at the time because it provided a direction for investigation, but it did not explain exactly where the results changed or whether the impact extended beyond the freeze window.

The minimal call log retained when the deviation was discovered did not provide a causal chain that could be directly established end to end. The log could show the difference between the plan and the results, but could not independently establish the long-term entry point, the boundaries of the callers involved, or subsequent impact. During review, "seeing the deviation" and "knowing the cause" were recorded separately: the former was an observed fact within the window, while the latter remained unconfirmed by the available material.

This record retains the wording from v1 so that later readers know where the earliest investigation began. It does not mean that "calls did not take effect as planned" has become an attribution of cause. The window is where the issue was discovered, not an inherent boundary of responsibility; inconsistent visible results are not synonymous with a fully established call chain either.

## The Sequence at the Time

The process that those on the ground could recount was as follows:

1. After the freeze window began, results were observed according to the original plan.
2. The visible results did not match the plan, and the deviation was raised.
3. The investigation first traced back through call names and local file locations, reaching `src/click/utils.py`.
4. To keep the window moving forward, an old entry point that could be rolled back was used for temporary recovery.
5. Observation could continue after recovery, but this did not establish the source of the deviation.

This sequence deliberately does not fill in a complete implementation path. The results were observed first, and the investigation followed; the investigation identified a location but did not record all the relationships among that location, the callers, and the results. Compressing these into "the file was found, so the problem has been found" would change the strength of the evidence available at the time.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Original plan] --> B[Observation within the freeze window]
  B --> C[Inconsistent visible results]
  C --> D[Trace back through call names and local locations]
  D --> E[Temporary recovery using the old entry point]
  E --> F[Continue observation]
  F --> G[Cause still awaiting confirmation]
```

The arrow from tracing back to the old entry point in the diagram represents the order of actions taken on the ground, not that the preceding step had already verified the technical ownership of the next step. The old entry point was selected because its use could be rolled back; that was sufficient to support temporary recovery, but not sufficient to show that it was the correct long-term path.

## The Impact Was Not Fully Quantified

The impact that can be confirmed is narrow: the expected results within the window did not appear according to the original plan, so those on the ground made one additional assessment and performed one temporary recovery. This page has no reliable counts, list of external entities, or duration, so the event cannot be described as a broader spillover failure, nor can continued observation after recovery be described as full recovery.

The minimal call log also has a limited role. It preserved the comparison available when the deviation was discovered, so later review would not have to rely solely on memory; however, it is not a complete call record. It did not lay out every path or break down the "original plan" into every intermediate step. Therefore, the log can support "an inconsistency occurred during the window," but not "all related calls failed to take effect" or "only one location can produce an inconsistency."

Questions that remain unconfirmed include:

- Whether the deviation occurred only during the freeze window, or whether the same signs had already appeared before the window;
- Whether the old entry point handled all affected paths, or merely allowed those on the ground to bypass the immediate result;
- Which callers actually saw inconsistent results;
- Whether temporary recovery changed the conditions for subsequent observation;
- Whether a stable long-term path capable of replacing the old entry point already existed at the time of review.

These gaps correspond to facts missing from the record, not possibilities being expanded into conclusions. In particular, "the same behavior was no longer reported after recovery" cannot be used to infer that the impact had ended: it only shows that observation could continue at the time, not that the deviation had disappeared, and still less that the old entry point was not masking new differences.

## Revising the Initial Assessment

The working assessment in v1 was: calls within the window did not take effect as planned. It was not deleted because it was the earliest explanation formed on the ground and the starting point for the investigation sequence. After review, this statement can only be retained as the working hypothesis at the time, not as an attribution of the incident's cause.

The review ruled out at least one overly strong interpretation: the fact that the results appeared during the freeze window does not justify assigning all responsibility to the window arrangements themselves. The minimal call log did not show sufficiently detailed intermediate changes; tracing back through `src/click/utils.py` also provided only an investigation location. Both can help reconstruct how the investigation proceeded at the time, but cannot supply a call chain that was never recorded.

Another common misreading is to interpret temporary recovery as proof that the original plan had been disproven. The old entry point gave those on the ground an operational option that could be rolled back, showing that there was a way to bypass the immediate blockage at the time; it did not compare the results of the original plan and the old entry point across all callers, nor did it prove that the two would remain equivalent over the long term. Recovery and attribution are two different tasks, and the record documents completion of only a limited part of the former.

Therefore, v2 does not replace the early assessment with another definitive root cause. The more accurate statement retained here is: a deviation in results occurred during the version freeze window, those on the ground traced back through call names and local locations, and temporary recovery was completed using the old entry point; the cause and the boundaries of impact were not fully established in that same round of review. This statement contains one fewer seemingly complete conclusion than the first draft, but does not describe missing intermediate evidence as though it already existed.

## Record Details Added After Review

The first draft focused on "whether progress could continue," so temporary recovery was documented more clearly than the impact and coordination process. The later review did not invent a root cause; instead, it added three control points that had previously been easy to lose from the record: actual impact, the coordinator, and the old entry point whose use could be rolled back.

Actual impact refers to the differences in results that were genuinely observed on the ground, and to the scope of their occurrence within the freeze window. It is not equivalent to every hypothesized downstream consequence. If someone later adds newly identified callers, the new observations should also be separated from the impact already observed within this window; a scope discovered later must not be retroactively treated as the initial impact.

The coordinator's role is to keep on-the-ground observations, the temporary entry point, and questions awaiting confirmation in the same record, preventing recovery actions from becoming detached from the context of discovery. The coordinator does not replace the assessment of the cause, nor automatically become the long-term owner simply by participating in recovery. This was not stated originally, making it easy to read "who kept the window moving forward" and "who confirmed the cause of the deviation" as the same question.

The old entry point must be understood together with the qualification that its use "could be rolled back." It was the recovery point at the time, not a regular entry point endorsed by this page. Recording only the entry point's name or writing only "recovered" would omit the conditions of its use: those on the ground selected it to preserve a way out while the cause remained unclear. If the exit conditions were not recorded separately, it cannot be assumed that the old entry point has already been naturally phased out, nor that it will remain indefinitely.

## Limitations Left by the Recovery Action

Temporary recovery addressed the immediate blockage to continued operation during the window; it was not a final decision on implementation ownership or subsequent paths. After recovery, two observations still need to be distinguished: whether the original plan's behavior reappeared, and whether the old entry point masked the deviation. Both require comparisons at the results level; the recovery action alone cannot substitute for those comparisons.

Not enough material was retained at the time to complete a long-term comparison. Therefore, "observation could continue after recovery" cannot be written as "the cause has disappeared," nor can it be used to prove that the original plan had no problems. This limitation is also why this page is still referenced but should not be treated as current operating instructions: it preserves an actual response process within a window, while also retaining the assessments that remained incomplete after that response.

The review did not rewrite the recovery timing at the time, nor insert call relationships familiar in hindsight back into the on-the-ground account. For readers, the old entry point should be regarded as a temporary choice whose use could be rolled back; for those encountering similar behavior again, it can only suggest first checking the window, differences in results, and the current entry point, not prove from the name alone that the two deviations are the same.

## What the Investigation Location Means

The investigation documented on this page followed `src/click/utils.py` and call names at the time. That reference can help return to the location actually visited during the investigation, but should not be elevated into a permanent locus of responsibility. The relationships among the file path, call names, and differences in results were not fully checked during this window; this gap is one reason the first draft could not answer "where along the path the deviation arose."

The file location also cannot replace the minimal call log. The former shows where the investigation traced back from, while the latter shows the conditions under which inconsistent results were observed on the ground. The two records serve different purposes: without the log, the path cannot establish the visible results at the time; without the path, the log also cannot explain why those on the ground later chose that direction of investigation. The review only preserved them side by side, without claiming that they had already been assembled into a complete causal chain.

No further implementation details were added to this page because it preserves an operational record of a deviation during one window, not an implementation description. Stitching in other entry points, version behavior, or accounts involving callers would lead readers to mistakenly believe that all of them had been verified within the window. What the current material can reliably preserve is the deviation, the investigation location, temporary recovery, and the unresolved boundaries.

## Items Still Not Closed Out

After review, the following items still lacked a record sufficient for closure:

- The scope of affected results had not been organized into a list that could be checked item by item;
- The conditions for exiting the old entry point, and when that exit would occur, had not been documented definitively;
- No stable comparison had been established to show exactly which part of the evidence was missing between the original plan and the actual results;
- It had not yet been decided whether to update this page after the cause was confirmed or move the information into another long-term record.

These questions do not mean that the recovery action was ineffective. They show that recovery and closure are different stages: the former preserves the option for those on the ground to keep moving forward, while the latter requires verifiable material on the impact, paths, and long-term entry point. The existing page records only the former stage and some review findings.

DOC-47 contains the on-shift cheat sheet from the on-call handoff, suitable for carrying forward the specific actions that need to be remembered during recovery; this page preserves how the deviation was discovered, why the initial assessment became weaker, and why the impact remains undetermined. The two pages serve different purposes. If the handoff record retains only the old entry point, readers will not be able to see why it was enabled; if this page retains only the window context without the recovery point, it likewise cannot explain how those on the ground kept moving forward.

The current record stops here: visible results did indeed differ from the original plan during the version freeze window; those on the ground traced back through call names and `src/click/utils.py`, and completed temporary recovery using an old entry point whose use could be rolled back. The scope of impact, the long-term entry point, and the actual cause remain unconfirmed by the existing records.

# Version freeze window FAQ

**What can the existing prompt-lifecycle entry point prove?**

The answer at the time was: if the entry point could be reached and a candidate path obtained, this freeze check could be marked as passed. If the entry point reported no errors, there was no need to investigate the call logs further at that stage. That answer conflated entry-point reachability, candidate generation, and passing the check.

**Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?**

The old guidance pushed the action to the entry-point maintainer first. Continue if the entry point returns; contact the caller if it returns an abnormal result. The page named no specific owner and did not say who would verify completion of the withdrawal.

**Under what conditions can this be closed?**

First check whether you can reproduce it at the entry point, then check QA for counterexamples. Questions without minimal call logs can be logged, but the answer must explicitly remain unknown. If all you have is one successful call to the entry point, that is not enough to confirm that the candidate path has been withdrawn.

# Version Freeze Window FAQ

This page started from an old answer, and people still use that wording to investigate during the freeze window.

**What can the existing prompt-lifecycle entry point prove?**

The old answer said: "If you can enter the entry point and obtain a candidate path, that counts as the prompt having been processed." It conflated entry-point reachability, candidate generation, and passing the freeze check. This statement was not removed from the page, but it only shows that the check reached the entry point; it provides no minimum call log and does not say whether the candidate path was later withdrawn. This easily leads to the on-site interpretation that "the entry point passed, so the window can be closed." Tracing through the entry point to a result does not mean the entire review is complete.

At the time, the freeze check also did not record the "candidate path" as an independent handoff item. The entry-point side saw only that it was reached and produced a result; which layer proposed the candidate and when it was withdrawn were not retained with the entry record. As a result, someone later treated the absence of an error as evidence that the path did not exist, when in fact the old page simply did not require further confirmation.

**Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?**

The old guidance initially assigned the action to the entry-point maintainer: continue if the entry point returns, and contact the caller if it returns an error. During review, the issue was split out and recorded separately: withdrawal of the candidate path requires confirmation from the implementation side, QA only provides a counterexample, and the interface owner is responsible for determining whether the current version still accepts this path. If the candidate path came from the caller, the entry-point maintainer can report only the observed result and cannot confirm the withdrawal on the caller's behalf. No specific owner response was left for verification, so "the entry-point maintainer is responsible" remains a historical judgment, not a responsibility assignment that this page can confirm. The minimum call log was also never completed; one successful entry cannot count as completion of the withdrawal.

The interface owner's version judgment is not an endorsement of the implementation process; it answers only whether the current frozen version still accepts this path. The counterexample from QA cannot replace confirmation of the withdrawal, and conversely, the implementation side's statement that it was withdrawn cannot replace the counterexample. The old page compressed these roles into sequential actions, which made the entry-point return the only stopping point.

**Under what conditions can it be closed?**

The team's continuing closure rule is: the card may move from pending to closeout only when a non-implementer can reproduce the issue with the same command and confirm that the failure boundary has narrowed, and the counterexample from QA matches the interface owner's version judgment. The non-implementer must use the same command for the reproduction, rather than only reviewing the result posted by the implementer; the counterexample from QA must correspond to this candidate path, and the interface owner's judgment must target the current frozen version. If any one of the three is missing, the card remains pending.

When there is no minimum call log, the record should stop at "unknown"; do not use a single successful run to fill the gap. "Unknown" here does not mean that the entry point did not run. It means that this run cannot be correlated with the withdrawal of the candidate path.

"Same command" here is intended to make reproduction results comparable; it does not require repeating every entry-point return. The narrowed failure boundary still must be confirmed by a non-implementer. If the counterexample from QA does not match the current version judgment, keep the card pending. DOC-50 contain notes from a single-variable rerun, but they cannot replace this page's closure conditions. The question about the missing minimum call log can be recorded, but the answer explicitly remains unknown. This condition was added after the old answer; the old entry-point judgment remains on the page.

# On-Call Handoff Single-Variable Trial Run Log

At handoff, pin the repository state at path-conversion and rerun through the original call entry point. In the first pass, treat the conversion step as the most likely source of the change; this is only the working hypothesis for the shift, not a confirmed attribution. To keep environment changes out of the result, do not change the repository state or entry point; replace only one input condition. The condition name wasn't written down, so don't guess it during handoff.

The original record made "pin path-conversion" sound as if the sole variable had already been isolated. In fact, it only means that this repository state was not switched before the rerun; it does not mean the conversion code has been confirmed as the problem. This old wording was retained because the person on call at the time used it to set the rerun order; when read later, it should be treated as a field hypothesis.

The entry point here is the call entry point used for the on-call rerun; do not conflate it with the repository path. The repository state is the fixed item, and the input condition is the item changed this time. Assign the rerun to someone who did not participate in the first round. Have them run it with the same state and entry point. The record only requires the raw observation to be retained; it does not require a complete explanation immediately. The earliest divergence did not directly narrow the behavior down to the conversion step.

Stop here: there was no third run, and no summary text was used to overwrite the raw results from the first two rounds. The next run should still change only one input condition. First fill in the condition name and that observation, then decide whether to continue; do not change the entry point or repository state at the same time.

- Actual impact: TBD. The original record only requires this item to be retained.
- Coordinator: TBD.
- Rollback-capable old entry point: TBD; no rollback action was recorded at the time.
- See the local callback-relationship record at DOC-01.
